# AlgebraicTypeType Call-Site Code Walkthrough

`crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/type_builders.ts` is a type export point in the TypeScript bindings. It puts names with different origins but related uses in the same file: public types brought in from `./algebraic_type`, as well as aliases that perform conditional inference for TypeBuilder, row, and column results. When you encounter a compile-time error, first identifying which category you are dealing with is usually faster than expanding the entire algebraic type definition first.

The code at the very beginning does not wrap `AlgebraicTypeType`:

```ts
export { type AlgebraicTypeType } from './algebraic_type';
```

This export is the most direct relationship between this file and `./algebraic_type`. Call Fang Ke to use this name from `type_builders.ts`, but the type declaration remains in the module being exported. The previous version classified it as a "possible construction entry point", which has now been corrected: what we see here is a type export point. `AlgebraicType` and `AlgebraicTypeVariants` are also imported from the same module, indicating that the builder types in this file interact with this set of algebraic type objects; this alone is not a reason to treat all three as the same type.

The declarations that can be located in the file appear in the following order:

```text
16  AlgebraicTypeType
21  InferTypeOfTypeBuilder
27  InferSpacetimeTypeOfTypeBuilder
33  Infer
42  InferTypeOfRow
49  InferSpacetimeTypeOfRow
58  CollapseColumn
```

This order is a guide for reading through the file, not a complete runtime call graph. The input boundaries of the first two TypeBuilder inferences can be identified directly from their signatures:

```ts
export type InferTypeOfTypeBuilder<T extends TypeBuilder<any, any>> =
export type InferSpacetimeTypeOfTypeBuilder<T extends TypeBuilder<any, any>> =
```

Both accept the same `TypeBuilder<any, any>` constraint, with the difference lying in the output side indicated by their names: one is `InferTypeOfTypeBuilder`, and the other is `InferSpacetimeTypeOfTypeBuilder`. When builder generics are not what you expect, first check whether the object passed at the call site satisfies this constraint, then check whether you need standard TypeScript inference or Spacetime-side inference. Substituting an arbitrary row object directly into these two aliases is not the starting point this file presents.

In the middle section, `Infer` shifts to row:

```ts
export type Infer<T> = T extends RowObj
```

The visible starting condition shows that this is not simply a new name for TypeBuilder. `InferTypeOfRow` and `InferSpacetimeTypeOfRow` follow immediately afterward, retaining two explicit entry points for the row scenario. When tracing types in practice, you can use the following branches as stopping points:

```text
The call site holds TypeBuilder
  ├─ TypeScript-side result → InferTypeOfTypeBuilder
  └─ Spacetime-side result  → InferSpacetimeTypeOfTypeBuilder

The call site holds a row shape
  ├─ General inference starting point      → Infer
  ├─ TypeScript-side row → InferTypeOfRow
  └─ Spacetime-side row  → InferSpacetimeTypeOfRow
```

This branching only describes the aliases' input categories and the adjacency of their names, and does not mean that these types execute in sequence at runtime. It also explains why `Infer` cannot replace the first two: its visible condition starts with `RowObj`, whereas the signatures of the builder-related aliases start with `TypeBuilder<any, any>`.

`CollapseColumn` is on line 58. It is close to the preceding row inferences, so when inspecting the resolved column type, looking back from it to the row-related aliases is a shorter route; if the only question is where `AlgebraicTypeType` comes from, there is no need to go through it first. The old notes listed `CollapseColumn` under the direct exports of `AlgebraicTypeType`, but the actual file order more strongly supports placing it on the column-results side.

There are also three groups of direct dependencies at the top of the file:

```ts
import { AlgebraicType, type AlgebraicTypeVariants } from './algebraic_type';
import type BinaryReader from './binary_reader';
import type BinaryWriter from './binary_writer';
import { ConnectionId, type ConnectionIdAlgebraicType } from './connection_id';
```

`BinaryReader` and `BinaryWriter` appear as type import statements, making them useful clues to the shapes used for binary reads and writes when reading the type declarations, but no particular read/write order should be inferred from these two lines. `ConnectionId` and `ConnectionIdAlgebraicType` appear together, indicating that the connection identifier has both a value-side name and a corresponding algebraic type name; when working with connection identifiers, make it a priority to keep these two names distinct.

The actual review sequence can be very short: first locate the target alias in this file; if it is `AlgebraicTypeType`, follow the re-export into `./algebraic_type`; for a builder or row result, keep track of the call site's input category, then choose the corresponding `Infer*` name; only consult `CollapseColumn` for column results. This avoids misreading public exports, conditional type inference, and binary-related dependencies as a single call chain.

One local follow-up item remains: the remaining conditional branches of `Infer` after `T extends RowObj`, and the specific resolution rules for `CollapseColumn`, are not expanded in the material excerpted on this page.

title: Timestamp UTC API proposal

versions.body:
# Timestamp UTC API proposal

First, a note on the two gaps we ran into on the API side at the time: with Timestamp in filter conditions, comparisons seemed to work, but the text representation hadn't been settled; at React procedure hook call sites, there was no consistent account of whether context belonged in the arguments, the return value, or outer state.

This isn't about immediately reworking a general-purpose time type. What we want to try now is to look at comparison and text output separately. On the comparison side, first check whether there is a numeric basis that can be made stable; on the text side, examine the UTC form on its own, so callers don't keep building filter conditions from an object's display output. When the two are mixed together, investigations end up mistaking "is it the same object?" for "are the conditions equal?".

`timestamp.ts` is the entry point noted so far. The file header shows `AlgebraicType` and `TimeDuration`, indicating that the time object isn't defined in isolation; we aren't treating that as a statement of React-layer ownership at this stage. There isn't enough material on the React procedure hook part yet, so it's being kept only as an adjacent item in the same review round.

Early assumption: if Timestamp display text is the same, the filters should be equal. This assumption makes it easy to build examples, but there are no counterexamples yet, and time zones, precision, and object construction paths haven't been considered separately.

The intent is to keep two lines of testing:

- whether comparison still yields the same condition for different objects constructed to represent the same instant;
- whether UTC text can be reused by the existing filter entry point without relying on extra processing in the display layer.

If the first requires object identity to hold, this proposal should be withdrawn and the observed behavior simply recorded instead; if the second can't maintain a consistent format, don't require the React hook to patch up the formatting either. For the hook context, we need to find another call site that can reproduce the argument order and returned state.

To add: the actual role of `TimeDuration` in this path; where context enters the React procedure hook.

versions.body:
# Timestamp UTC API Proposal

The previous version treated Timestamp's display text as the basis for comparison, but that claim did not hold up on review. Display text is the result a reader can see; it does not establish which value the filter condition used. Identical text is also no substitute for checking the internal time values. The original passage is retained because that was the direction the experiment initially took.

## Initial notes

At the time, we judged only by the name next to `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/timestamp.ts` and assumed this was mainly a formatting issue. The file imports `AlgebraicType` and `TimeDuration` at the top, but we did not trace the call chain from there. The early plan called for settling on a UTC format first, then checking whether the filter could reuse it.

That plan had an obvious gap: it did not answer what should happen when two different Timestamp objects represent the same instant, or whether six decimal places were a display preference or part of the condition's semantics. We did not document that gap at the time, so later discussions used "comparison" and "printing" interchangeably.

## Working assumptions after review

The problem is now framed in two layers.

The first is value comparison. The proposed approach no longer starts from object references; instead, it looks for an existing numeric representation of Timestamp to use as the basis for comparison. The benefit is that callers would not have to retain the same object instance; the trade-off is that we need to confirm that the numeric representation uses the time unit accepted by the filter.

The second is conversion to text. The UTC string should be stable, observable output, not a string filled in on the fly by React or a consumer. If the string is correct only in logs but follows a different path during condition construction, the two will diverge sooner or later.

These two layers do not need to be implemented by the same code. `timestamp.ts` can handle the local work around type adjacency and time-value conversion; the filter entry point is responsible for writing the established value into the condition; the React procedure hook only needs to ensure that its context has not replaced the condition with a different object wrapper. At this stage, the hook is not being designed as an entry point for time formatting.

## Old approach, retained but no longer pursued

> Previous assessment: compare Timestamp objects first, then generate the filter condition from the object's display text.

This passage is obsolete. It excludes cases involving two objects constructed for the same instant and makes display logic responsible for condition semantics. It is retained not for continued use, but to explain why the earlier checks covered only the case of passing the same object repeatedly.

The old check is also no longer a pre-release step: create an object, pass that object straight back, and check whether the displayed string is unchanged. This only shows that passing the reference once did not change the display; it does not show that the filter can still match across construction paths.

## Proposed narrow adjustment

The initial scope is limited to Timestamp equality conditions and their UTC text. The candidate implementation does not change the public roles of `AlgebraicType` or `TimeDuration`, nor does this round of work attempt to unify all time operations. The only things to verify are that independently constructed Timestamp objects for the same instant are not treated as distinct on the condition side merely because they are different objects; that text output retains enough precision to distinguish microseconds; and that callers do not need to supply a time zone or zero-padding themselves.

The criteria for withdrawing the proposal are also narrow: if numeric comparison would change the meaning of existing non-equality filters, or if the UTC text cannot retain a consistent form at the existing condition entry point, stop pursuing this approach and do not extend the formatting rules into the React procedure hook. At that point, return to the call site to determine which layer is actually rewriting the time value.

## React procedure hook side thread

This remains unresolved, but it is already clear that it should not be tied to Timestamp object comparison. What needs checking is not "whether React supports time," but which parameters the context available to the procedure hook currently contains, what return state it retains, and whether the condition object is rebuilt before or after it enters the hook.

There is not yet enough evidence that the context comes from a fixed provider, nor is there evidence that it has a direct call relationship with `timestamp.ts`. The proposed inspection order here is therefore: first record the argument order and return state at the actual procedure call site; if that site already has a complete condition object, trace back through the construction of the time value; if it has only raw input, keep condition generation outside the hook.

## Where to record follow-up findings

Append follow-up examples to this page first; do not split object identity, UTC output, and hook context into three scattered conclusions that cross-reference one another. Wait until we have a counterexample involving independent construction before deciding whether the proposed approach warrants moving ahead with an API adjustment.

versions.body:
# Timestamp UTC Interface Proposal

When this page was first recorded, time filtering and the React procedure hook were placed on the same worksheet. Both appeared around the interface review, but they were not the same kind of problem: the former concerned which instant a condition ultimately represents, while the latter concerned what context the call site passes to the procedure. Over the years these two threads were written together several times, then separated again several times; these traces are being preserved, so that anyone reading the old examples later can tell which conclusions apply only to the construction methods used at the time.

The code entry point that can still be traced is `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/timestamp.ts`. The file directly imports `AlgebraicType` and `TimeDuration` at the beginning. These two neighboring objects are enough to show that Timestamp handling is more than just string formatting, but they cannot replace checking the actual references. Material related to the React procedure hook is examined separately through call-site entry points; the two topics being adjacent on this page does not mean that either side owns the other side's implementation.

## Early Notes: First Make the Examples Look Consistent

The earliest notes had just one very simple goal: to make the time in the filter look like UTC text. The examples at the time came from repeatedly passing the same Timestamp object, and the only observation was that the object's display did not change within a single call. The notes therefore described "the display is the same" as "the condition is the same", and suggested first making the displayed results consistent, then addressing comparison.

That reasoning now looks insufficient, but it explains why some people later asked about format first, rather than value. Those notes did not distinguish three different actions: creating a time object, writing it into a filter condition, displaying it as text. The three actions happened to yield similar results in one simple example, so they were treated as the same thing.

An unfinished side note was also left at the time: whether `TimeDuration` would participate in turning Timestamp into a condition. There was no answer, and there is no need to fill it in using later results. It simply reminds readers, given the time-related neighboring types already present along this path, not to attribute all differences to UTC text.

## Addendum to the First Review: Objects Do Not Define the Boundaries of Conditions

In subsequent reviews, the discussion shifted from "whether strings need zero-padding" to "whether two independently constructed objects can represent the same condition". This led to the first line of counterexamples: if a comparison can hold only for the same object instance, the caller will reach different conclusions after deserialization, state transfer or reconstruction, even if they refer to the same time.

The working hypothesis proposed at the time was that comparisons should be based on the numeric value represented by Timestamp, rather than on object identity. This hypothesis did not bring all time operations into scope. The scope covered only equality filtering; sorting, range conditions and duration conversions outside that scope still needed to be verified individually. The scope was narrowed this way, because "unifying time behavior" would turn an issue that could otherwise be verified locally into a round of interface rewriting.

Another idea also came up in the review: have the React procedure hook normalize the object, then pass the normalized value to the filter. The advantage of this idea is that callers have one less step to perform; the disadvantage is that the hook would start taking on temporal semantics that do not belong to it, while non-React call paths would still need separate handling logic. This idea was not pursued further as a solution.

## An old set of steps still retained here

The old steps below were once used for manual verification. They are no longer suitable for assessing interface semantics, but their original intent is preserved:

1. Create a Timestamp;
2. Pass the same object directly into condition construction;
3. Compare the object's displayed text with the generated result;
4. Then pass the same object to the procedure call.

This set of steps can only demonstrate that passing the object directly once did not change the visible result. It does not reconstruct the object, nor does it force the time value out of the current reference, so it cannot detect identity comparisons. The text seen in step three may not be the text ultimately used by the condition layer, either. The old steps were valuable at the time because they first revealed that the display and the conditions might come from different places; but they should no longer be treated as a release criterion.

## A change in direction from a review

The later review did not keep asking "which object lives longer," but instead split the checks into two sets of inputs. The first set keeps the same object to confirm that the original direct-passing behavior has not been broken; the second set constructs separate objects for the same instant to rule out accidental passes due to reference identity. This shift was small, but it changed how the problem was read: instead of first asking whether the strings look alike, first ask whether the conditions still point to the same instant.

The text aspect was also kept separate in this review. UTC output is not just a pretty format for logs; it is a form callers can observe and copy, so its precision and time zone must not vary arbitrarily depending on the entry point. On the other hand, text cannot in turn define object equality. The two layers can cross-check each other, but they do not follow the same rule.

No complete call graph was recorded at this stage. The available material only supports starting from `timestamp.ts` to inspect its local declarations and navigate to adjacent items; it cannot be used to assign broader responsibilities to `AlgebraicType`, `TimeDuration`, or the React procedure hook. What is missing is not some terminology, but where values are brought into condition construction at the actual call site.

## A few pages of scattered notes about the hook

The React procedure hook was listed as an adjacent issue in this round of work for a practical reason: someone saw time conditions at a procedure call site and also needed to check the parameter order and the actual returned state. Early notes mistakenly assumed that "hook context" was a single object; later additions did not support this claim.

The issue should be broken down more specifically here. We need to know: in what order the arguments passed into the hook appear at the call site; whether the state returned by the hook preserves the state actually seen by the caller; and whether condition objects are rewrapped as they enter or leave this layer. If the call site has already received a complete condition, the hook should not rewrite the semantics of time comparisons. If the call site retains only the raw input, condition generation should be placed closer to time-value conversion, rather than relying on the display output from the React layer.

Someone once suggested using the UTC text as the hook's stable interface, on the grounds that it would be easier for the frontend to print and debug. This suggestion was not adopted. It would combine the values needed by conditions, the text needed by the UI, and the procedure's context into a single container, hindering comparisons involving independently constructed objects and depriving non-React callers of the same entry point.

Therefore, the approach retained on this page is not to "add a time adapter to the hook", but to first treat an inventory of the hook's context as a separate task. It shares part of its review history with the Timestamp changes, but not implementation responsibility.

## Overturned statements

> Previous conclusion: As long as the UTC text for Timestamp is the same, the two objects can be treated as the same filter value.

This statement has been overturned. It treats visible text as the equality relation itself, without handling cases where the two objects come from different construction paths. It is retained because many older examples appear correct precisely because they rely on passing the same object directly through; removing it would instead leave readers unsure what those older examples covered.

> Previous conclusion: The React procedure hook is an appropriate place to standardize time formats.

This statement is also no longer applicable. The hook needs to preserve the calling context, not decide the format and comparison method for time conditions on behalf of all callers. If a particular hook call site is found to actually reconstruct condition objects in the future, that site's inputs and outputs should be recorded before deciding whether a local patch is needed; it must not first be elevated to a unified entry point.

Another old plan was never carried out: attributing all differences in UTC text to time zones. Precision can also affect how distinguishable conditions are, especially for time values within the same second. The old plan focused only on the trailing time zone indicator and overlooked the fractional part, so it is no longer used as the troubleshooting sequence.

## Current candidate changes

The candidate changes remain limited in scope: equality filtering for Timestamp should be based on the time value it represents; the UTC text serves as a stable external representation of that value; the React procedure hook is not responsible for converting object identity or display text into condition semantics.

This has two direct benefits. First, callers do not need to retain the original object instance to obtain the same filtering result. Second, the responsibilities of conditions and text can be verified separately: the former checks independently constructed values for the same instant, while the latter checks whether the time zone, zero-padding, and precision are stable. It also has a clear cost: the implementation must clearly distinguish between internal time values and text output, and cannot rely on a single implicit conversion to satisfy both sides.

The proposed checks still center on two minimal examples. Example A passes the same Timestamp object directly into condition construction; retain it to prevent regressions in the old path. Example B uses two Timestamps constructed independently for the same instant and requires that equality conditions not distinguish between them merely because they are different objects. No additional range comparisons or date arithmetic are success criteria for this adjustment.

Text examples should be observed where conditions are generated, rather than only through UI or logs. If one caller displays a Timestamp as UTC, while another caller generates text with different precision at the filtering entry point, the problem should not be interpreted as a "frontend display difference"; verification needs to return to the point where time values are converted into conditions. The React hook is not required to reproduce every textual form here, only to avoid introducing another set of condition semantics.

## Disagreements during review

In a supplemental review note, the more conservative proposal was to continue accepting objects passed directly and only add the UTC form for the current display. This has a small change surface and does not touch numeric comparisons. But it does not address equality after values cross boundaries; it merely keeps the existing examples looking good.

Another proposal was to immediately unify all Timestamp operations, including equality, ranges, sorting, and duration calculations. This is conceptually tidy, but goes beyond the known problem. Ranges and sorting each have their own endpoint semantics, and duration is also closely related to `TimeDuration`; changing everything at once would turn verifiable local compatibility into a large change that is hard to diagnose.

The current choice is the middle approach: first tighten the relationship between equality filtering and UTC text, while retaining the existing paths for other operations. This choice is not based on a belief that the other paths have no problems, but on the fact that the existing counterexamples and review records only provide enough support for this area. If the equality-filtering adjustment reveals that range conditions share the same conversion, propose follow-up work separately.

The conditions for backing out are also explicit. If comparing by time value causes existing equality conditions to produce different results for the same input, and the difference cannot be traced to object identity or the construction path, stop the merge rather than hiding the results with text formatting. If UTC text cannot maintain fixed precision on the condition side, also stop using it as a source of examples that can be copied. If evidence from the React procedure hook proves that conditions are rebuilt at this layer, treat that case as a separate fix target rather than turning the hook into a global time adaptation layer.

## The card entry point for the year 2025

SDK-202 later used the shortest existing regression example as the entry point for checks, with the focus still on Timestamp filter comparisons and UTC text. The card is a good starting point for investigating public examples, but the card itself does not replace the earlier assessments and correction process preserved here. When revisiting this, first confirm whether the example involved independent construction, then inspect the condition output, rather than merely looking for logs of a particular object.

SDK-219, in turn, records the current inventory of React procedure hook Context's dependents. The subsequent public addendum still notes that one context remains unconfirmed, so this page does not present it as a completed compatibility conclusion. You can follow this card to the call site to check the parameter order and actual return status; any new local observations should be added to the hook thread, rather than retroactively treated as evidence that Timestamp has already changed.

The two cards have different dates, and the later hook inventory must not be backfilled into the Timestamp experiments from earlier years. When the early notes did not yet have these two entry points, all that could be done was to record the issues and candidate approaches; the card numbers are retained now so maintainers can find the call sites still in use.

## Current wording conventions

Following the earlier legacy examples, the object-identity counterexample approach, text layering, and the inventory of the hook side thread, the following now serves as the requirement for closing the interface review: Timestamp equality filtering compares by microsSinceUnixEpoch rather than object identity, and UTC strings retain six decimal places; the example filter must appear verbatim as createdAt = '2024-01-01T00:00:00.123000Z'.

This requirement addresses only equality filtering and its corresponding text representation. It does not change all operations on `TimeDuration` to follow Timestamp rules, nor does it claim that the React procedure hook has completed its context migration. When using this example, the column name, spaces on both sides of the equals sign, single quotes, six decimal places, and the UTC suffix are all part of the output; do not change it to another approximate form for log display.

Implementation checks can proceed in this order: first, use the path containing `timestamp.ts` to confirm where the local conversion of the time value occurs; then pass distinct objects representing the same instant into equality filtering; finally, check the UTC text at the condition output. If the call chain passes through the procedure hook, also record the parameters it receives and its return status, but do not reassess equality within the hook based on the display text.

Here, "by microsSinceUnixEpoch" describes the basis for equality filtering, not a requirement for callers to manipulate that value directly. Callers can still use Timestamp objects; the change is that, when an object enters a condition, equality no longer hinges on whether it is the original instance. This preserves object-level usage while also preventing condition semantics from changing across boundaries.

## Issues not yet split out

The one unresolved point about the React procedure hook's context remains noted here. The known task is to inventory consumers and preserve the argument order and actual return status at the call site; what remains unknown is whether the condition object is reconstructed there or an existing object is merely passed through. Without that finding, no stronger compatibility commitment can be made for the hook.

Another related question is which layer produces the UTC text. The current requirements constrain the results visible to the filter, which does not mean that every UI display must go through the same function. If a presentation layer is later found to have reduced precision, first determine whether it participates in condition generation; a purely presentational difference should not automatically be expanded into a change to filter semantics.

`AlgebraicType` and `TimeDuration` are still treated only as direct neighbors visible in the header of the `timestamp.ts` file. They are worth keeping in mind when making changes, but this page does not contain enough material to list them as targets for changes in the current proposal. If numerical comparisons are later found to pass through either one, record that actual path and its impact separately, rather than inferring relationships here based on names alone.

## Archived Excerpts

The key point from the early review can be condensed into one sentence: first find counterexamples that bring different construction paths together, then decide whether the display text is part of the condition. This sequence later replaced the approach of "making the strings look nice first".

The additional note on the hook is more restrained: one entry in the consumer inventory remains unconfirmed, and the existing CLI call site cannot be used to infer that all React calls retain the same context. This reminder remains valid, because it prevents a local observation from being written up as a complete design decision.

## Old Examples Appendix

### Old Example One: Round-Tripping the Same Object

The old example creates a Timestamp and passes it directly into condition construction, and copies the displayed result into manual notes. This example can still be used to check for obvious regressions in the direct-passing path, but it cannot serve as the only example for equality filtering. It does not produce a second object, nor does it cover cases where the object is reconstructed across a call boundary.

### Old Example Two: Formatting Before Comparison

Another old example first converts the object to UTC text, then uses that text as an approximate basis for comparison. That example is outdated and should no longer be used for interface checks. Its only remaining value is this reminder: text conversion and comparison were once incorrectly coupled, so precision, time zones, and object identity were not validated separately.

### Old Example Three: Unified Handling on the hook Side

An old draft envisioned having the React procedure hook accept any time value and output uniform text. This idea was not included in the current proposal. It would make the calling context responsible for both formatting and condition generation, and would also leave a second set of behaviors for non-React paths. By retaining this example, we aim to avoid reintroducing the same mixed responsibilities later in the name of "reducing work for callers".

Any material added later should stay focused on the specific thread it addresses: Timestamp value comparison, condition-side UTC text, or the context at the hook call site. Do not describe all three as a single generic "time compatibility" issue again.

# Index metadata and write troubleshooting tree

When an index entry is missing from a table definition, or someone calls a post-write anomaly "storage reuse," first record the two symptoms separately. The old record points to `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/table.ts`; use it here only as a starting point for checking objects near the table definition.

The working assessment at the time was that field-level indexes would be included with `columns`; the table-level declarations in `options` seemed to be additional descriptive information. If an item is missing from the schema result, first check whether `options` is still present, then check `columns` for similar fields. If both sides are present but an item is still missing from the result, first save the original declaration and result. Do not change a table-level item to a field-level item just to make the result look complete.

```text
Index result is missing entries
├─ Only the index name is available
│  └─ Add options or columns for the same table
├─ Declaration present in options; columns not obtained
│  └─ Fill in the field-side information first; do not change the original declaration
├─ Similar fields in columns
│  └─ Record the similarities; do not merge the two types of items
└─ Both sides present, but the result is still missing entries
   └─ Save the result object; investigate the parsing location later
```

The top of the file has type imports for `ProcedureExport`, `ReducerExport`, `t`, and `errors`, as well as a value import for `BinaryWriter`. These only help decide what to open next. They do not establish what produces the index result, nor do they prove that the write anomaly went through the writer.

On the write side, only collect observations at this stage. A return value or exception after a single write is not enough to establish that storage was reused; if the words "index" and "write" both appear in a report, keep the two pieces of material separate. Still missing: a call snippet that shows the table-level declaration, field indexes, and parsing result together.

# Index Metadata and Write Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally put "an index is missing from the schema" and "after a duplicate write, it looks like old content was brought back" on the same troubleshooting path. A later review found no object linking the two. The old entry point is still retained, but start by following separate paths based on the observations.

## Earlier guidance retained here

The earliest record pointed to `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/table.ts`. At the time, field indexes and table-level indexes were treated as roughly equivalent forms: when `columns` already contained a similar field, the table-level item in `options` seemed not to need separate tracking. This conclusion came from a cursory look at declaration locations; the complete parsed set was not saved.

The old tree is below; it is no longer suitable as a fix path:

```text
Missing index item
├─ A same-named or similar field already exists in columns
│  └─ Assume the field item will override the table-level item
├─ Only some properties are visible in options
│  └─ Assume omitted properties can be ignored
└─ The result object cannot be obtained
   └─ Change the caller's declaration shape and retry
```

The last branch is especially problematic. Rewriting the caller prematurely combines the two input surfaces that originally needed to be compared into one. After that, it is impossible to tell whether the declaration changed, parsing omitted something, or the result was displayed incompletely. The old note still directs people here, so the tree was not deleted; when you encounter the same description, do not follow it to flatten the table-level declaration.

## Later on-call note

Two narrowly scoped notes were left in the margin of the on-call page: a missing-index report must include `options`, `columns`, and the result object; a write anomaly must include the actual object used in the call and the observed result. Without these materials, record only the observation; do not state "the same cause."

When the report concerns an index, first ask which layer is missing: the original declaration, the parsed schema, or the result seen by the consumer. If all you have is one name or a screenshot, you cannot determine whether it originally belonged to the field side or the table-level side. Similar names are not a substitute for provenance.

```text
The report concerns an index
├─ The same table has options and columns
│  └─ Compare the two declaration types, then inspect the result set
├─ Only options
│  └─ Stop: provide columns; do not move the table-level item
├─ Only columns
│  └─ Stop: provide options; do not use the field side as a substitute
└─ Only a result description
   └─ Stop: provide the original object
```

When the report concerns a write, first confirm that the reported case actually reached the writer path. A single operation can record only what was returned or thrown; "reuse" requires at least two operations and evidence of object continuity. In `table.ts`, there is `import BinaryWriter from './binary_writer';`, so writer is an adjacent entry point that can be investigated further, but an import is not a call record.

```text
The report concerns a write
├─ Only one operation
│  └─ Record the observation; stop attributing a cause
├─ Repeated operations exist, but the object is unclear
│  └─ Provide the objects and results from both operations
├─ Entry into the adjacent path for BinaryWriter can be confirmed
│  └─ Continue investigating on the writer side
└─ An index description is included as well
   └─ Return to the index tree; do not use metadata to explain it
```

## A review attempt that did not pan out

During the review, we tried to split responsibilities quickly based on the import list: put `ProcedureExport`, `ReducerExport`, and `t` on the server-adjacent side, put `BinaryWriter` on the write-adjacent side, and treat the table file as the intermediate junction. This split did not answer where `options` was interpreted, nor whether the index items in the result came from field or table-level declarations.

The failure points left at the time were:

- Only `options` was copied; `columns` for the same table was not retained;
- Only index names were checked; whether an algorithm or uniqueness appeared in the declaration was not recorded;
- An anomaly after a single write was seen, and the title was set to storage reuse;
- We tried to infer the source of the anomaly from the type import of `errors`, with no usable result.

The troubleshooting sequence was therefore temporarily narrowed to keeping the declaration, parsed result, and write observation in separate branches. If a branch has no original object, mark it as not reviewed; do not fill it in with material from another branch.

## Structure for next time

```text
Suspected missing table-level declaration
├─ options or columns are missing
│  └─ Provide the original declaration for the same table
├─ Both are present, but the layer cannot be determined
│  └─ Mark each item as coming from the field side or the table-level side
└─ Both item types are distinguishable, but the result still lacks items
   └─ Check where the parsed result is generated

Suspected storage reuse
├─ Only a single write result
│  └─ Record only the single-operation observation
├─ Repeated operations, but object identity is unclear
│  └─ Provide the object and the results from both operations
└─ The writer-adjacent path has already been entered
   └─ Recheck writer; do not treat a missing index item as a prerequisite
```

Still needed: one snippet showing a table-level declaration, a field index, and a parsed result together; one record of repeated operations showing clear entry into `BinaryWriter`.

# Index Metadata and Write Troubleshooting Tree

When this page is dug up near the table definition, it usually carries two unrelated but easily co-written descriptions: index entries in the schema or metadata do not match expectations; after a write, someone suspects that old storage was reused. Early records connected them into one thread, and only later were they gradually split apart. The old entry point is still `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/table.ts`, but the entry point itself does not imply that these two phenomena are related.

The file header shows type imports for `ProcedureExport`, `ReducerExport`, `t`, and `errors`, as well as a value import for `BinaryWriter`. They are useful for deciding the first step in tracing back: table-definition issues should stay near table, and only issues confirmed to have entered the write object should continue to writer. Do not treat the import list as object ownership or a causal chain.

## 2023-06-05: The initial split

The initial record focused on "an index entry is missing." The judgment at the time was crude: indexes on fields were introduced by `columns`, while table-level indexes were merely another kind of description in `options`; if similar column names appeared on both sides, retaining only the field side did not necessarily warrant further investigation. This judgment did not obtain the complete parsed index set, much less compare the table-level declaration's own properties.

The tree from that time is retained below. It explains why some old comments recommended changing the caller first, but it can no longer serve as the current action.

```text
Index entry missing
├─ columns contain similar fields
│  └─ First merge the table-level item into the field item
├─ options show only some properties
│  └─ Assume properties that were not written out can be ignored
└─ schema result is incomplete
   └─ Adjust the caller, then observe again
```

The main problem with this tree is not that a particular step will necessarily trigger an exception, but that it changes the object being observed before observation. If the table-level item is rewritten as a field item, it is no longer possible to distinguish afterward whether the original declaration was complete, whether parsing dropped an item, or whether the result object originally displayed only one side. The original section is retained because some table definitions in early screenshots had already been changed this way; deleting it would make those screenshots appear to have no explanation.

There was also a marginal note from the same period: "When index results are unstable, also check whether writer reused the previous storage." It was merely an association created by putting the two terms together. The original record did not specify the write object, call order, or intermediate results, nor did it provide a connection from metadata to writer. The note was not removed later; instead, it was demoted from an operational entry point to a historical misdiagnosis.

## 2023-06-06: Stop Points at the Edge of Review

The following day's review did not fill in the implementation details; it only stated more clearly where the on-duty person should stop. An index issue should include the two input surfaces of the table definition; a write issue should include the actual object involved. When the material is incomplete, first keep the original fragment; do not use "the same root cause" to fill in the gaps.

When the report says "the index is gone," first ask which layer they mean:

- It is absent from the declaration itself;
- The declaration is still there, but it cannot be seen in the schema or metadata;
- The metadata is still there, but the result obtained by the consumer does not meet expectations.

These three answers are not the same issue. An index name cannot identify its source. Even if the name is the same as a field, that is not enough to conclude that it came from `columns`, much less to delete the item from `options`.

When the report says "the buffer was reused again," first ask whether this came from a single write or a repeated operation. With only one operation, at most record the returned value or the thrown content; that is not enough to describe reuse. If there really were two operations, it is also necessary to know whether the two operations were looking at the same object. Without object continuity, the anomaly should not be written up as the writer holding data from the previous round.

```text
A short incident report comes in
├─ "The index is missing"
│  ├─ Only a name or screenshot
│  │  └─ Stop: add options, columns, or the result object
│  └─ A complete table definition is available
│     └─ Record the field side and table-level side separately
└─ "Write reuse"
   ├─ Only one result
   │  └─ Stop: record only the single-occurrence symptom
   ├─ Two results, object unclear
   │  └─ Stop: add the call object
   └─ The writer call can be confirmed
      └─ Switch to the writer adjacency path
```

Here, "stop" does not mean closing the issue. It only means that without the input object, a verbal description may not be upgraded into a parsing failure or storage policy. This stop point was retained later because it was easier to preserve the reproduction conditions than the earlier instruction to "first change it to column-level retry."

## 2023 Year-End: The Import-List Shortcut Did Not Work

A review attempt assigned path responsibilities using the import list. `ProcedureExport`, `ReducerExport`, and `t` were treated as server adjacency; `BinaryWriter` was treated as write adjacency; someone therefore provisionally assumed that the table file merely connected the two sides and would not affect how the index results were formed.

This inference was not supported by the result object. The imports only indicate what is visible near the file header; they do not show where `options` is interpreted, nor whether a parsed index entry comes from a field declaration or a table-level declaration. The review also tried to infer the source of the anomaly from the type imports for `errors`, but again produced no output useful for troubleshooting.

The failed-attempt notes left in the draft at the time were as follows:

- Only `options` was saved, without also saving `columns` for the same table;
- Comparisons were made only by index name, without retaining the column set, the algorithm, or whether uniqueness was specified;
- There was only one write result, yet the behavior was called "storage reuse";
- Responsibilities were assigned to objects based only on imports, without examining the parsed results in detail;
- Because the report mentioned both indexes and writes, it was assumed that the two shared a single trigger.

This review did not produce a fix, only a narrower correction: the index path starts with whether declarations are retained; the write path starts with which object is actually entered. The two paths may appear in the same issue report, but that does not mean they can explain each other.

## The crossed-out shortcut approach

The approach below was once treated as a time-saving sequence of steps. It is now marked **deprecated**. The old record is retained to explain why some historical diffs left only field-level entries.

1. When table-level entries are missing from the results, first rewrite the same columns as field-level indexes;
2. If the results appear to be restored, assume that table-level declarations do not need to be retained;
3. If they are still inconsistent, then check `BinaryWriter`;
4. If the writer side cannot be opened for the time being, classify the issue as caching or reuse.

Steps one and two change the shape of the input. Steps three and four have no chain of observations linking the index results to the writer. The problem with this approach is that it neither preserved the declarations nor obtained write-related material; it appeared to shorten troubleshooting, but actually obscured both unknowns.

After the old approach was deprecated, reports should at least retain the original locations: table-level entries stay in `options`, and field-level entries stay in `columns`. Even if the two ultimately produce the same index semantics, that should be assessed only after the parsed results are visible, rather than merging the inputs first. The same applies to the write side: proceed to the implementation adjacent to the writer only after confirming that the object being examined has an actual call relationship with `BinaryWriter`.

## An on-call incident record

One record put "the declaration was at table level, but only field-level entries remained in the results" and "after repeated writes, there was a suspicion that old content was still visible" in the same paragraph. The review did not obtain enough call-related material, so it did not confirm whether the two occurred at the same time, much less whether one caused the other. All that could be retained were two separate observation requirements:

- The index branch preserves `options`,`columns` and the shape of the index entries in the parsed result;
- The write branch preserves the object used for the calls, along with what each operation actually returned or threw.

Internal tracing of writer was not completed at the time of the incident. When revisiting this section later, do not automatically read "after writing" as "`BinaryWriter` has reused storage". Without evidence of two operations and object continuity, the "reuse" in the old heading is only a description to be verified, not an attribution of the failure.

```text
First choose a branch based on the symptoms
├─ schema / metadata index inconsistency
│  ├─ Complete table definition not obtained
│  │  └─ Add the options and columns for the same table
│  ├─ Both types of declarations are present
│  │  └─ Check whether the parsed result still distinguishes their sources
│  └─ metadata is still present, the consumer still reports an error
│     └─ Retain the object the consumer received, do not recast this as missing entries in the parsed result
└─ Abnormal object or result after writing
   ├─ No explicit writer call
   │  └─ Do not attribute the issue to "reuse"
   ├─ Only one result
   │  └─ Record the result, stop at the single operation
   └─ Two operations and their objects can be compared
      └─ Go back and check what the implementation adjacent to writer actually retains
```

The tree's two root nodes are presented in parallel, solely to prevent the old report from conflating them. This does not mean that the metadata branch of table and the storage branch of writer share an implementation path.

## Corrections in the Intermediate Revision

The intermediate revision changed "field indexes override table-level declarations" to "check the two side by side". This was better than the original framing, but still not specific enough: it did not specify how to evaluate the result set, nor did it address the default value when uniqueness is not specified. At the same time, it scaled the characterization of `BinaryWriter` back from "the cause of the anomaly" to "adjacent navigation visible in the table file".

This correction resolved a common misreading. The presence of `import BinaryWriter from './binary_writer';` only means that a value import is visible in that file. It is not enough to prove that the current behavior passed through writer, nor is it enough to show that writer retained the contents of the previous operation. When missing index entries and a write anomaly appear in the same message, first separate the message into two observations; without new evidence, do not draw a connecting line between them in the record.

The intermediate revision also left one branch unresolved: where to continue investigating when the index entries are still present in metadata but a consumer only consumes field entries. There is not enough call-related evidence here to determine which implementation is responsible. This page only requires retaining the declarations for the same table, the parsed result and the object the consumer actually received, to avoid once again using "not retained during parsing" to obscure a different kind of problem.

## Review Panel: Where Synthesis Happens

There were two opinions during the review. One opinion held that table-level declarations would ultimately also become index results, so they should be synthesized as early as possible during troubleshooting, making the path shorter. The other opinion held that synthesis may occur in the implementation, but troubleshooting records must not be synthesized first at the input layer; the same column may have field-side information and may also participate in a table-level declaration, and merging them early would lose the reference for missing items.

The latter opinion was retained. It does not mean that field indexes and table-level indexes are always mutually exclusive, nor does it replace the reading method of a specific implementation. It only specifies the record order: retain the source hierarchy first, then compare the parsed sets. The review did not decide the writer's storage rules, nor did it assign the write issue to the table branch.

There is also one unresolved comment in the review: if metadata is complete but the usage result does not match, which layer should take over. This page did not use that as a basis to invent an owner or a call edge. During on-call, just leave the object seen by the consumer alongside the metadata; only then can a follow-up review distinguish a consumption issue from a parsing issue.

## Current index verification

The statement below replaces the earlier statement that "table-level items can be ignored." It applies only to index declarations in the table definition and parsing results; it does not extend to the storage lifecycle rules of `BinaryWriter`.

table(options, columns) table-level index declarations must explicitly provide accessor, algorithm, and columns; tablesToSchema's resolvedIndexes retains both field indexes and table-level indexes, and uses unique false when uniqueness is not declared.

When starting from a symptom, first determine whether the complete declaration for the same table has been obtained. If `options` is absent or `columns` is absent, that is insufficient for layer-level attribution. Once both are present, first label each item as field-side or table-level, then inspect the `resolvedIndexes` obtained from `tablesToSchema`. Do not collapse the two categories early just because the column names are similar; do not rewrite missing table-level items on the field side just to continue checking.

When the table-level item itself is missing `accessor`, `algorithm`, or `columns`, the issue stops at declaration completeness; fix the declaration itself first. Once all three are specified, check whether the result set retains both the field index and the table-level index. When uniqueness is not provided in the declaration, result verification must see `unique false`; the omission cannot be treated as room for the caller to decide on its own.

```text
The index declaration does not match the result
├─ Missing options or columns
│  └─ Stop: provide the original table definition
├─ Table-level item is missing accessor / algorithm / columns
│  └─ Stop: declaration incomplete; fix this table-level item first
├─ The two source types are clear, but the result has fewer items
│  └─ Retain options, columns, and resolvedIndexes; then inspect parsing
├─ The result contains both field items and table-level items
│  └─ Check the column set, algorithm, and unique
└─ metadata is complete, but the result seen by the consumer still does not match
   └─ Retain the consumer-side object and continue checking on the consumer side
```

This tree does not require every similar name to be treated as a duplicate. The relationship between the field side and the table-level side should be determined from the parsed objects. If a table-level declaration involves multiple columns or includes a description that the field side lacks, backfilling it into `columns` based only on a single-column name will lose the original semantics. Investigation records should preserve the input's original position.

## The write side is still only sufficient for triage

`BinaryWriter` is still worth retaining as a follow-up entry point because the table file imports it directly; however, no evidence has been obtained here that can describe writer's internal storage rules. For "storage reuse," the actionable step at present is to separate the evidence into layers, rather than define a reuse mechanism on this page.

```text
Suspect BinaryWriter Storage Reuse
├─ The phenomenon appears only in schema or metadata results
│  └─ Return to the index tree; do not attribute it to writer
├─ There is a writer-related call, but only one result
│  └─ Record the return value or exception; stop at that operation
├─ There are two operations, but it cannot be confirmed whether they involve the same object
│  └─ Add the object identity, then compare the two results
└─ The two operations and object continuity are both clear
   └─ Check the actual retained content in the implementation adjacent to binary_writer
```

Do not treat "reuse" as synonymous with any write anomaly. It requires evidence of repeated operations and object continuity. Conversely, missing items in the index result do not automatically mean that the write side has ever run. The two trees are on the same page because old reports often put them together, not because a common root cause has already been established.

## Issues still outstanding

The first outstanding item is still on the consumer side: metadata already retains the table-level item, but when the consumer reads only field items, the current evidence cannot say which call site should be modified. It is sufficient to retain `options`, `columns`, and `resolvedIndexes` for the same table, along with the consumer object; an import relationship cannot replace a call record.

The second outstanding item is object continuity in the writer branch. If later work obtains only the exception text and not the objects from the two operations, the record should revert to "single-operation phenomenon on the write side," and storage reuse should no longer be used as the basis for judgment. This narrowing is more useful than carrying over the old title because it preserves the gap needed for the next review.

## Legacy Examples Appendix

**Legacy Example One: Changing a table-level item into a field-level item.** This approach was once used to make the results look uniform. It made the original `options` declaration disappear, so it later became impossible to distinguish a parsing change from rewritten input. This example no longer applies; it is retained only to explain the shape of a historical diff.

**Legacy Example Two: Inferring writer responsibility from an import.** An old note treated `import BinaryWriter from './binary_writer';` as sufficient reason to conclude that the anomaly came from writer. It is now treated only as adjacent navigation; the existence of an import does not mean that the current symptom passed through this call edge.

**Old Review Excerpt.** One conclusion left at the time was "Preserve the source first, then discuss merging." It was later put into practice as follows: the field side and the table-level side must not fill in for each other before `resolvedIndexes`. The write branch is outside the scope of this conclusion and still needs its own operational materials.

**Retained Text Samples.** The old verification page once kept two rendered texts side by side to confirm that the table fields and time conditions had not been distorted during copying: `SELECT * FROM "person" WHERE "person"."active" = TRUE` and `createdAt = '2024-01-01T00:00:00.123000Z'`. They are not attribution materials for the index or writer and cannot replace the declarations and object records required by this page.

The page still retains an old note at the end: if someone comes back with only the description "both indexing and writing are wrong," first ask them to choose a tree. When neither tree has enough objects, leaving two unreviewed items is closer to what happened at the time than inventing another common cause.

# Decision on authentication context and Range exports

These two issues were considered together during the same compatibility wrap-up: callers of TypeScript needed to describe the authentication context, and a server-side requirement to export Range/Bound had also come up. The initial draft took a conservative view based on the situation around `crates/bindings-typescript/src/server/runtime.ts`.

The decision at the time was to hold off on separately expanding type exports for the authentication context. The runtime could already receive authentication-related values, and the inconsistent sample behavior looked more like differences in how callers understood the return shape; adding context fields directly to public types before stable samples were available would lock in an unstable shape.

Range and Bound were also provisionally treated as objects internal to Server Runtime. They could appear along server-side paths, but no call sites requiring direct access from the top level of SDK were recorded here, so the decision was not to add any new standalone exports.

The verification starting point remains `crates/bindings-typescript/src/server/runtime.ts`. The file header brings in both values and types from `spacetime:sys@2.0`; any later attempt to overturn the assessment above should start there to confirm exactly at which layer authentication values and range objects leave the runtime.

Open: whether authentication-related values need stable type names; whether Range/Bound has any independent server-side consumers.

# Authentication Context and Range Export Decision

This record puts the authentication context and Range/Bound together because, when things were initially wrapped up, both fell under a judgment near Server Runtime: on one side, whether authentication-related values should have a type for TypeScript callers to write against, and on the other, whether the range objects had already constituted an export available for server-side use. In retrospect, this categorization makes it easy to assume they are the same interface issue; at the time, the boundaries between the two were not separated.

The initial draft's conclusion was simple: there was no rush to add a separate type for the authentication context, and no rush to add separate exports for Range and Bound. The runtime path already exposed authentication-related values, and range objects could also appear during server-side operations; at the time, there was no call-site material sufficient to fix the public surface. Thus, both issues were treated as caller integration that had not yet converged, rather than as runtime omissions.

This conclusion remains here because it did guide that round of handling. It does not state which fields the authentication context has, where Range or Bound can be imported from, or constitute a compatibility commitment for server-side calls. Treating this record as an interface reference table would be more likely to cause misuse than deleting it.

## The trade-offs at the time

There were two approaches to the authentication context.

The first was to quickly organize the authentication values visible at runtime into a public type and have callers write parameters, callbacks, or helper functions around that type. This would let examples use a unified name sooner, but once the fields, nullability, and source were fixed, even a local adjustment to the server's internal representation would create an external compatibility burden.

The second was to retain the current runtime state and handle only call sites that could already be confirmed. The initial draft chose the second approach. The reason was not that it had confirmed the authentication context should never be exported, but that it could not determine which shape should be exported at the time. The initial draft attributed inconsistencies in the examples to the usage side and therefore did not list a type export as a blocker.

For Range/Bound, there were also two options on the table. One was to treat them as part of the server-side API: whenever callers needed to construct, pass, or identify a range, there should be a stable import location and name. The other was to keep them near the runtime, for use only by code already on that path. The initial draft chose the latter, on the grounds that "the server can encounter the objects" was insufficient to infer that "SDK should expose the objects externally."

These two deferrals were not exactly the same. The authentication context issue was that the type shape had not been finalized; the issue with Range/Bound was that the export layer had not been finalized. The old draft combined them as "do not export for now," making it easy during later review to use one item's handling to explain the other.

## The locations relied on at the time

The stable entry point left behind was:

`crates/bindings-typescript/src/server/runtime.ts`

At the top of the file, the value side and type side both connect to `spacetime:sys@2.0`:

```ts
import * as _syscalls2_0 from 'spacetime:sys@2.0';
import type { ModuleHooks, u128, u16, u256, u32 } from 'spacetime:sys@2.0';
```

The initial draft understood this section as Server Runtime handling both system calls and type declarations, so it traced both the authentication type and the range export back here. This entry point is suitable for checking direct runtime adjacency, but it cannot alone determine the boundary of the public API; the old draft did not make this distinction clear.

Value imports only show that the runtime depends on system interfaces, while type imports only show that the source file needs to spell out certain system types. They cannot guarantee a public type for the authentication context, nor prove on behalf of Range/Bound that a server-side export already exists. The initial draft effectively treated "visible in the same file" as "should be handled at the same layer," which is precisely the mistaken assumption that should still be preserved in the record.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> RuntimeObservation
    RuntimeObservation: Observation near runtime.ts
    RuntimeObservation --> DeferredType: Authentication type deferred
    RuntimeObservation --> DeferredRange: Range/Bound export deferred
    DeferredType --> Recheck
    DeferredRange --> Recheck
    Recheck: Follow-up review
```

The diagram does not show implementation flow, but the initial draft's judgment path. Both branches stopped in a deferred state at the time; it does not indicate that the authentication type and range export had already been designed uniformly, nor that the runtime file had authority over all interface decisions.

## What the initial draft actually left behind

The initial draft did not deny the existence of the authentication context. It conflated "the runtime can obtain authentication-related values" with "calling Fang Ke to reference a stable type" and then prioritized the former. This avoided naming things too early while the fields were unknown, but it also did not record what callers actually needed to express.

The initial draft also did not deny that the server had range operations. It merely treated Range/Bound as an object on the runtime path and mistook the fact that code near the current file might access the object for a reason to keep it internal. If callers needed to construct or pass ranges through the SDK surface, this decision did not answer where the export should reside.

The boundary at the time can be reconstructed as two statements:

- Before confirming how callers would write it, do not fix the type shape of the authentication context.
- Before confirming whether server-side callers need an independent import, do not add an export for Range/Bound.

These two statements describe a deferral position, not a design principle. They were later read as "no action needed," which is the most obvious source of misleading interpretation in this record.

## The retained old approach

The initial draft once used the following handling approach, which was not deleted later:

> If authentication calls can still run, do not add a context type for now; if range operations can still be completed through the server-side path, do not establish a separate export for Range/Bound. Let callers compare the differences between examples themselves.

This passage treated successful runtime execution as evidence that a type export was unimportant, and treated the fact that an operation could be completed as evidence that the export layer did not matter. Both inferences skipped the question of whether callers could write, import, and maintain it consistently.

However, deleting it would make people mistakenly believe that a complete public API design had already been compared at the time. In fact, it had not. The initial draft merely made a conservative choice near a local runtime entry point and left the unverified parts for later example cleanup. This background explains better than a complete conclusion written after the fact why the issue was not split apart when things were wrapped up.

## View after the addendum

The review did not establish a new public interface choice on this page; it only restored the distinction missing from the old decision: the authentication context first requires confirmation of the shape seen by callers, while Range/Bound first requires confirmation of whether server-side callers need an independent entry point. Neither can be decided merely because an object name or an authentication-related term appears near the runtime.

Therefore, `crates/bindings-typescript/src/server/runtime.ts` remains as a recheck entry point. Here, one can continue tracing Server Runtime's direct integration with system interfaces, along with the adjacency between authentication-related values and range objects. It is no longer treated as the sole home of the authentication type or Range/Bound.

When discussing a public type for the authentication context, the runtime value must first be separated from the way callers write against it. The fact that the runtime side can receive a value alone cannot determine the type name, field set, or import location. If Range/Bound is to be discussed as an export, the first step is to separate internal server-side passing from callers constructing it themselves; the former's existence does not automatically answer the latter.

The connection to DOC-20 is only that both materials recorded questions around the same round of interface review. DOC-20 deals with byte-view reset and server function Registration Context, and cannot be used in place of the authentication or range assessment here.

## Unanswered questions

- If the authentication context needs a type export, which layer constrains the relationship between the runtime value and the public type.
- When Range/Bound appears in the server-side path, whether callers need to construct or import them themselves.
- If both objects ultimately become part of the public surface, whether they should be at the same export layer.

These questions still had no conclusions at the time of the last addendum. The old decision is retained not because it is reliable, but because it records the deferred path taken at the time and the distinction that path failed to make.

# Byte View and Function Registration Proposal

This draft separates two issues that were mixed together in one interface review: Byte View reset Boundaries, and the context retained when registering a server function. The first concerns the area around `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/binary_reader.ts`; for the second, we'll first look at two points in existing calls: registration and execution. We won't combine them into a single change at this stage.

## Limited reset prototype

Start by reading the same byte view repeatedly. Record `offset`, `byteOffset`, and `byteLength` before and after reset, then read once more. Check whether the reader's position has returned to the start and whether subsequent reads still use the original view. The earlier assessment was that reset probably only needs to set the read position to zero and should not rebuild or modify the byte view. This assessment does not yet cover views with a nonzero `byteOffset`, so we can't finalize the interface on that basis.

There are two candidate approaches. One is to update only the current position within BinaryReader; the other is to reacquire the readable view on reset. The first is a narrow change and better matches existing callers' expectations about the view's bounds; the second looks like an easy way to avoid leftover state, but would mean reinterpreting the bounds of byteOffset and byteLength. Try the first approach first. If the next read after reset goes outside the original view, or the caller can see a change to the view's contents, revert this localized change and keep the existing read sequence.

## Assumptions about registration context

Registration and actual execution of a server function may not happen within the same call. The draft lists two tentative approaches: save the context needed for execution at registration time, or retrieve it again from the entry point at execution time. Saving it would make execution less dependent on entry-point state, but the proposal has not yet addressed repeat registration, invalidated objects, or cleanup after a failure; retrieving it again would store less state, but could lose information visible at registration time when execution is asynchronous.

We won't take the "add a copy of the context at both points" approach in this round. That would make it impossible to tell, when a failure occurs, whether reset changed the read bounds or the registration state was overwritten. First, use the existing examples to trigger registration and execution separately and identify the minimal context actually visible at each point; if the two contexts differ to begin with, stop pursuing the save-context approach and do not use defaults to paper over the differences.

## Open questions

- Whether views with a nonzero `byteOffset` may continue to be reused after reset.
- Whether there is any local state to clear besides the reader's current position.
- Which values the minimal registration context should contain.
- Whether to reject repeat registration at the registration point or let the later registration replace the earlier one.

At this stage, the only recommendation is to validate byte reading and the registration path separately. Once these questions have answers, decide whether changing the public interface is worthwhile.

# U32 Round-Trip and Subscription Readiness Troubleshooting Tree

First split reports into two categories: a numeric value differs after being written and read back, or a subscription has been established but readiness hasn't progressed as expected. Don't combine these two symptoms into one conclusion; they were only raised together in the compatibility train.

## Numeric Round Trips

When a report involving U32 Little-Endian Round-Trip Compatibility comes in, first retain the original input and the value read back. If the reporter only says "there's an encoding problem," first ask whether the written bytes differ from expectations or the numeric value read back differs from expectations. Until those two cases are distinguished, don't attribute the issue to the write side or the read side.

The provisional investigation entry point is `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/binary_writer.ts`. This file is related to binary writes; its header shows:

```ts
import { fromByteArray } from 'base64-js';
```

This only helps locate nearby objects to inspect. The base64-related imports alone don't explain the byte order and can't be treated as the cause of a round-trip failure.

- Raw bytes are available: first compare the order of the written bytes, then check the value read back.
- Only the value read back is available: ask for the write-side bytes or a reproducible example.
- Only "a particular caller is incompatible" is reported: record the call site first; don't use that to draw conclusions about all write paths.

Stop condition: without at least two of the input, bytes, and value read back, don't attribute the issue to little-endian handling.

## readiness

On the subscription side, first clarify what "not ready" means: did it never enter readiness, or was it observed as not ready after entering it? If there is no record of state changes, only note that the state machine needs investigation.

- The subscription is known not to have been established: keep investigating the path before subscription establishment.
- The subscription has been established but readiness hasn't progressed: preserve the sequence of events between establishment and observation.
- readiness has changed but the caller still considers it not ready: record the caller's observation point; don't rewrite this as a state machine failure.

Do not use numeric round-trip examples here to explain subscription issues. Keep evidence for the two investigation paths separate, and wait for verifiable examples before assessing them together.
