# U32 Round-Trip and Subscription Readiness Troubleshooting Tree

This record originally put the U32 round trip and subscription readiness on a single issue ticket to make it easier to collect reports; after review, triage should still branch by observed symptom. The numeric path needs the bytes, and the subscription path needs the state changes. The two types of evidence cannot substitute for each other.

`crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/binary_writer.ts` remains the entry point for tracing back the binary side. The direct dependency in the file header is:

```ts
import { fromByteArray } from 'base64-js';
```

This import indicates that the file is near base64 byte handling, but it does not establish the byte order of U32. During troubleshooting, use it only as the starting point for looking around BinaryWriter; the call names in the report still need to be checked individually.

## From Reports to Branches

When a "round-trip incompatibility" report comes in, first write down three things: the U32 value before writing, the bytes written out, and the value read back. If any one is missing, two completely different descriptions may be conflated.

```text
U32 report
├─ Pre-write value, bytes, and read-back value available
│  ├─ Byte order does not match expectations → keep it on the write side
│  └─ Bytes confirmed, but read-back value does not match → keep it on the read side
├─ Only the pre-write value and read-back value
│  └─ Request the bytes; do not assign byte-order responsibility yet
└─ Only "caller failure"
   └─ First record the call site and sample; do not fold it into all paths
```

A "little-endian round trip" includes at least two observable points: the write and the read. Matching final numeric values alone does not show that the intermediate byte arrangement was checked; a byte sequence alone does not show that the reader accepted it. If the same sample behaves differently in two environments, first save the three observations from each environment side by side; do not use environment names in place of actual values.

If the reproduction material contains only one common numeric value, do not immediately generalize it into a claim that all U32 instances fail or all pass. The current ticket description requires using an existing test or example to trigger U32 Little-Endian Round-Trip Compatibility, and writing the uncovered user paths back to SDK-208. Here, "uncovered" is a gap in the report material, not a default path that can be filled in by guesswork.

An action record already exists for the interface review of SDK-208; it then moved into processing, making it suitable as a navigation point for the numeric path. It does not replace checking the bytes for each sample.

## Keep a Separate Record for the Subscription Path

A single "not ready" statement can easily send the readiness investigation off track. First distinguish these observations:

1. The subscription has not been established;
2. The subscription has been established, but no readiness progression was observed;
3. Readiness has progressed, but a subsequent observation again showed it as not ready;
4. The caller did not obtain the result it expected, but there is no state-change evidence.

The first three are different branches. The fourth can only be treated as material still to be supplied; it cannot be used to select any branch directly.

```text
Subscription report
├─ Establishment action not completed
│  └─ Record which establishment stage it stopped at; do not discuss readiness transitions
├─ Established, but no readiness progression observed
│  └─ Preserve the order of establishment completion and observation
├─ Progression observed, later considered not ready
│  └─ Preserve both observations; do not compress them into "never ready"
└─ No state-change record
   └─ Request a state observation; stop here
```

Do not use a passing numeric test to close the subscription branch. A U32 round trip can show that a binary sample has been checked, but it does not show that Subscription readiness State Machine went through the same call path. Conversely, a subscription report cannot be used to determine the byte arrangement of BinaryWriter.

## Field Record Format

Each piece of evidence only needs to be attached under one branch:

- the exact wording of the symptom;
- the pre-write value, bytes, and read-back value, or subscription establishment and state changes;
- whether the sample came from a test, an example, or the caller;
- the branch already ruled out, and the basis for ruling it out.

Do not turn both report types into the same table just to make them look tidy. The numeric side centers on the bytes in the round trip; the subscription side centers on the order of states. When there is not enough material, retain "bytes to be supplied" or "state change to be supplied."

## Boundary After This Review

The review did not identify a common failure point that would allow the two topics to be combined. The earlier wording—"both may be caused by the binary layer"—is no longer used: reports on subscription readiness do not provide material that would place it under `binary_writer.ts`. The binary file remains the entry point for the U32 branch; continue collecting subscription-branch material according to state-machine observations.

If a new U32 sample can provide the input, bytes, and read-back value together, first check it within the scope of SDK-208. If a new subscription report can show the order of establishment completion and readiness, organize it under the subscription branch; do not assemble unconfirmed content into a recovery explanation—stop at the observable point instead.

# U32 Round-Trip and Subscription Readiness Troubleshooting Tree

During the compatibility train, U32 Little-Endian Round-Trip Compatibility and Subscription readiness State Machine often appear in the same batch of reports. They share a reporting window, not a confirmed implementation-level cause. When handling them on call, first separate them by observable symptoms; cross-reference them in the records only when the same evidence can explain both paths.

The starting point for follow-up checks on the binary side is still `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/binary_writer.ts`. The file header shows:

```ts
import { fromByteArray } from 'base64-js';
```

This information is useful for directing people to look around BinaryWriter, not for inferring byte order, readback logic, or subscription behavior. Some past reports attributed readiness to the write layer as well based solely on the filename, but when they were reviewed later, no state evidence supporting that attribution had been retained. That assessment was withdrawn, but the original report categories are retained below to help identify which part is missing.

---

## Choose an entry point first, not a cause

When an issue is reported, first determine which category the material submitted by the reporter falls into:

```text
Observable symptoms in the report
│
├─ "The value read back after writing is incorrect"
│  └─ Go to the U32 round-trip branch
│
├─ "The subscription is not ready" or "Something is wrong again after it becomes ready"
│  └─ Go to the readiness branch
│
├─ Both statements appear, but neither bytes nor state changes are provided
│  └─ Split into two records awaiting more information; do not attribute them to a common cause
│
└─ Only a call name, a filename, or a one-line compatibility assessment
   └─ Request the minimum observational evidence before proceeding
```

The minimum evidence here does not have a fixed format. On the U32 side, at least two observation points in the round trip must be visible; on the subscription side, at least the relationship between setup and state observation must be visible. If the report only says "It worked before, but it does not work now", that statement can only help pinpoint the perceived regression; it cannot replace inputs, bytes, or the sequence of states.

When handling the issue, do not start by asking "Is it BinaryWriter". First ask "Which fact has already been observed". Working hypotheses may be retained in the on-call records, but they must be placed under the corresponding branches and corrected as new evidence arrives. This prevents whoever takes over later from misreading an as-yet-unverified identification of a file as a confirmed root cause.

## U32 Round-Trip Branch

### Three pieces of evidence to retain

U32 Little-Endian Round-Trip Compatibility involves at least the value before writing, the bytes after writing, and the value after reading. Evidence from the incident does not have to include complete screenshots or the full test context every time, but it must be clear which part is missing.

| Available material | What can be determined | Stopping point for this round |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-write value, bytes, read-back value | The discrepancy can be investigated further on the write side or the read side | Stop attributing the cause if all three cannot be matched to the same sample |
| Pre-write value and read-back value | Can confirm that "the round-trip result was reported as abnormal" | Request the intermediate bytes; endianness cannot be determined |
| Bytes and read-back value | Can examine the read-back observation | Not a substitute for the actual value before writing |
| Bytes only | Can only retain the byte sample | Do not claim that a round-trip failure occurred |
| Caller description only | Record the call location or example name | Do not generalize it to all call paths |

"U32 Little-Endian Round-Trip Compatibility" is not just a matter of putting the three-character label "little-endian" on a report and calling it done. For a specific sample, both the write side and the read side must refer to the same input. If the pre-write value comes from one example, the bytes from another log, and the read-back value from a third caller, this material can be retained temporarily, but it cannot be pieced together into a confirmed round trip.

### When material for all three stages is available

First, arrange the three observation points in order of occurrence: the original U32 value, the bytes written, and the U32 value read back. Then branch just once.

```text
Value → bytes → value
├─ The bytes written already differ from what is expected for this sample
│  └─ Keep the material on the write side and inspect objects near BinaryWriter
├─ The bytes written have been confirmed, but the read-back value does not match
│  └─ Keep the material on the read side; do not recast the issue as a write error
├─ All three stages can be matched, and the results are consistent
│  └─ This sample passes; do not use this to close reports from other callers
└─ All three stages have the same name, but their sources cannot be matched
   └─ Return to "matching information still needed"; do not choose either side
```

The BinaryWriter entry point comes into play in the first branch: when the byte observation itself shows a discrepancy, start at `binary_writer.ts` and inspect the nearby code. The `fromByteArray` import at the top of the file only indicates that there is a base64-js dependency there; do not automatically equate the base64 form, buffer representation, or textual appearance in the report with the byte order of U32. If the material cannot link the textual representation to the actual bytes, byte evidence is still needed.

If a complete sample has already confirmed that the bytes written match expectations, continue collecting material on the read side. At this point, do not go back and ask BinaryWriter to account for the issue just to keep things neatly organized as "one issue per file". Checking one entry point does not mean another entry point has also been checked.

### When bytes are unavailable

The earlier draft directly classified "the pre-write value and the read-back value differ" as a little-endian issue. That approach no longer applies. This can show that the round-trip result warrants attention, but it cannot show whether the discrepancy arose before writing, during writing, in transit, or during reading.

The current procedure is shorter:

- Retain the pre-write value and the read-back value;
- Indicate whether these two values come from the same sample;
- Request the missing bytes produced by the write;
- Do not conclude that there is a "byte-order error" before the bytes are available.

Do not assume default values, a default environment, or hidden call paths just to fill in missing information. If the caller can provide only a final value, the record can remain marked "awaiting bytes"; it is still a valid starting point for investigating an anomaly, but is insufficient to assign it to either the write side or the read side.

### Handling a sample after it passes

A passing U32 sample only shows that, based on the available observations, there is no discrepancy in that particular round-trip chain. It does not automatically cover other user paths. The card description for SDK-208 requires using existing tests or examples to trigger U32 Little-Endian Round-Trip Compatibility, and writing any user paths that remain uncovered back to the card.

Therefore, when recording a pass, state at least: whether this was a test, an example, or caller-provided material; which two or three stages were observed; whether any paths remain uncovered. Do not write "existing tests passed" as "all paths are compatible", and conversely do not invalidate a specific passing sample just because an uncovered path exists.

Later actions on SDK-208 included interface review and starting work. It is a suitable place to collect new samples and gaps on the numeric side. The action status on the card does not mean that a particular byte sample has been reviewed; the observations of the three stages in the document remain the basis for assessment.

### Stop conditions for the numeric branch

Stop broadening the conclusions if any of the following occurs:

1. The original value, bytes, and read-back value cannot be tied to the same case;
2. Only the call name is available, with no observable input or output;
3. The bytes appear in some textual form, but their relationship to the write result cannot be confirmed;
4. The report presents the subscription not being ready alongside a numeric discrepancy, but does not explain which came first or how they are related.

Stopping does not mean discarding the report. Retain the originally reported behavior and gaps, and wait for additional material; do not turn "awaiting more information" into a seemingly complete conclusion about the binary data.

---

## readiness branch

For Subscription readiness State Machine's report, the first step is not to look for traces of numeric encoding, but to break down what "not ready" means. In practice, this term may mean that the subscription has not yet been established, that no readiness progress has been observed after it was established, that readiness had previously progressed but the subscription was later observed to be not ready again, or simply that the caller is dissatisfied with the result they received. These four descriptions are not interchangeable.

```text
Subscription observations
├─ Subscription not yet established
│  └─ Record the point at which establishment stopped; readiness is not yet part of the current assessment
├─ Established, but no readiness progress observed
│  └─ Preserve the order of establishment completion and the observation time
├─ Readiness progress observed, then later shown to be not ready again
│  └─ Preserve both observations; do not abbreviate this as "never ready"
├─ Caller result does not meet expectations, but no status record
│  └─ Treat it as a caller observation; require the status change to be added
└─ Report contains only "there is a problem with the state machine"
   └─ Do not choose one of the above branches for the reporter
```

### Subscription not yet established

If the material shows that the subscription was not established, stop at the establishment path first. Calling the problem a readiness failure at this point would cause subsequent checks to skip a necessary prerequisite. The record should clearly state the observation "establishment did not complete," rather than broadly summarizing it as "ready never arrived."

This branch does not require invoking the U32 sample, nor checking `binary_writer.ts`. The binary side happens to have an unresolved report, which will not answer whether the subscription was established.

### Established but no progress observed

If the subscription has been established and the material shows that no readiness progress was observed, preserve the order of the two facts: establishment came first, followed by the observation of no progress. Do not rewrite this as "the state never changed" unless the report actually provides enough continuous observation to support "never."

The most common gap is that only the final interface or the caller's description is retained, while evidence that establishment completed and a status observation are missing. In this situation, the record should stop at "the order of establishment and observation needs to be supplemented." This is more useful than saying "it may be the state machine," because once the missing material is added, a branch can be selected directly.

### Progressed once, then considered not ready

This branch requires retaining two observations: readiness progressed, and later it was again observed to be not ready. Do not reduce this to "never became ready"; otherwise, subsequent investigation may mistakenly assume that only initial establishment needs to be checked. Nor should you unilaterally interpret it as a state rollback, a cache issue, or caller misreading; the current material only allows us to confirm the observation order first.

If the caller only remembers "it was fine just now, then it stopped working later," classify it as pending information for this branch rather than treating the memory as a complete timeline. The pending item should specify whether the missing piece is the first progression or the later not-ready observation, rather than vaguely writing "more logs are needed."

### Only the caller's result

The caller Fang Ke can report that a particular operation did not produce the expected result, but provides no record of any change in subscription establishment or readiness. This is valid integration-testing feedback, not direct evidence of a state-machine problem. When recording it, preserve the caller's observation point and require the following to be added: whether the subscription has been established, when readiness checking began, and what status changes were observed.

Do not fill in these states for the report just because SDK-225 is about Subscription readiness State Machine. SDK-225 is the navigation entry point for this type of issue; it cannot turn environments, default files, or state progressions that have not been provided into established facts.

### Stop conditions for the readiness branch

In the following cases, only record the information; do not attribute a cause:

- No observations related to subscription setup;
- No readiness state changes;
- Only the caller's final result is provided;
- U32 is also mentioned, but its relationship to the subscription observations is not explained;
- The two state observations come from different cases, with no explanation of how they are related.

When stopping, preserve the original wording. Do not rephrase "state changes not provided" as "state machine anomaly", since the latter already implies a judgment that the evidence has not yet supplied.

---

## When both paths are mentioned

It is not uncommon for the same report to mention both numeric round-tripping and a subscription not being ready. Process them in the following order:

1. First, place the U32 evidence in the "value—bytes—value" sequence;
2. Then place the subscription evidence in the "setup—state observation" sequence;
3. Indicate whether there is an explanation showing that they come from the same case, share the same sequence of events, or are directly related;
4. If no relationship is explained, keep two separate records.

Do not write "U32 caused readiness not to advance" or "the subscription issue caused anomalous U32 read-back" merely because both phenomena were reported in one test. Such causality requires additional evidence, while the responsibility of the current troubleshooting process is to preserve verifiable boundaries.

Older records used "the binary layer may affect subscriptions" as a label to make tracking easier. That label can explain why the two types of reports were grouped together at the time, but it is no longer used as a current triage rule. Now, add a relationship note only when the report explicitly states the connection between the two sides; even then, the numeric branch and the state branch each retain their own observation points.

---

## How to write up field evidence

The evidence does not all have to be put into the same table. U32 is best recorded in terms of the numeric value, bytes, and read-back value; subscriptions are best recorded in terms of setup and state changes. Forcing a uniform format will cause byte information to be written as abstract states, or state ordering to be misrepresented as a sequence of values.

The numeric side can use the following minimal record:

```text
Sample:
U32 before writing:
Bytes written:
U32 read back:
Whether all three come from the same case:
Current branch:
```

The subscription side can use the following minimal record:

```text
Case:
Whether the subscription is established:
Order of readiness observations:
Caller observation points:
Current branch:
```

Fields may be left blank. Blank fields make it easier to move the next review forward than answers filled in based on impressions. For reports that already have supporting material, there is no need to copy all the historical background again; only add the new values, bytes, state sequences, or caller observations from this round.

If a piece of evidence comes from an existing test or example, simply state clearly whether it belongs to a test or an example; there is no need to treat it as representative of the entire compatibility surface. If it comes from a caller, record only the observations that caller actually provided. This way, when SDK-208 and SDK-225 receive subsequent additions, it will be clear which content is observed fact and which branches still need supporting material.

---

## Corrections from the latest review

The second version of this page already separated the numeric path from the subscription path, but it still retained an ambiguous statement: as long as the area around BinaryWriter was checked, the subscription side could be closed out as part of the same review. That statement is not valid.

Locating `binary_writer.ts` only serves the U32 branch where byte differences occur. The subscription readiness branch requires evidence of establishment and state changes. Both sides can be handled in the same round, but their completion criteria differ:

- The U32 side is based on round-trip observations for the same example;
- The readiness side is based on the order in which subscription establishment and state changes are observed.

Therefore, when a numeric example passes, close only the numeric checks already covered by that example. If subscription state evidence is insufficient, remain on the subscription branch. Conversely, a clear sequence of subscription observations does not replace the intermediate bytes of U32.

SDK-225 already has historical actions for risk review and the start of processing. New readiness evidence can be routed back to that card according to the branches on this page; the card is used to bring the items together, while actual judgments must still be based on the establishment and state observations recorded on this page. Do not treat card action names as the result of a state-machine reproduction.

---

## Only these items need to be left at handoff

When a branch cannot proceed for now, the handoff should be brief and allow work to continue:

- U32: which parts are already available (pre-write value, bytes, read-back value), which parts are missing, and whether they belong to the same case;
- readiness: whether the subscription has been established, the known order of state observations, and which observation is missing;
- If both are reported together: whether there is actual material linking them, or they merely appeared in the same batch;
- Which side of SDK-208 or SDK-225 the new material should go back to.

There is no need to include a generalized conclusion. The next person handling this should be able to proceed directly to the appropriate branch based on these four types of information: if there are byte differences, continue near BinaryWriter; if subscription establishment and the state order are available, continue reading the readiness branch; if the material is insufficient, specify exactly which item needs to be added.

## Items still requiring additional material

- SDK-208: coverage of user paths not yet covered should be written back once actual tests or examples become available, not replaced with existing passing examples.
- SDK-225: subscription establishment and readiness observations in reports need to be stored separately; records containing only caller-side results are still insufficient to select a state machine branch.
- Between the two cards: there is currently insufficient material to establish a common cause linking the U32 byte round-trip and subscription readiness.

# Boolean Decoding and table clear Migration Workflow

This page initially kept two compatibility-track projects in the same record, simply because both needed review after the upgrade. Later field review split this write-up apart: fast Boolean decoding must track exactly how many bytes a read consumes, while table clear must track what a bigint parameter retains after passing through the binding layer. The two tracks can share one migration window, but they cannot share observation results, replacement decisions, or recovery criteria.

The old entry points and old working criteria are retained below. They are still useful for bringing people back to the original troubleshooting locations; parts that are no longer sufficient to support replacement are corrected later without being deleted.

## The Two Tracks Initially Left Behind

The early draft had just one working assumption: first confirm whether the Boolean value is correct; if the result is correct, the read call can remain unchanged for now. This assumption was later narrowed. The Boolean value is only one result in a sequential read segment; if the read end position differs, adjacent fields may still begin at the wrong position, and comparing true or false alone cannot rule out a consumption offset.

table clear was also written at the time as a post-upgrade cleanup result regression. This phrase is retained as the issue entry point, but it is too coarse. When the cleanup result changes, at minimum the pre-upgrade parameter, post-upgrade parameter, and value actually received by the binding layer must be distinguished. Otherwise, differences in parameter passing and the final result can easily be conflated as the same kind of anomaly.

The old investigation pointed from `internal/TSDK`'s `v_prev` to the following location:

```text
crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/binary_reader.ts
```

This path is the search entry point for the Boolean track, not a statement of table clear implementation ownership. After opening it, start with the Boolean-read adjacency around `BinaryReader`, then return to the callers that actually use the fast read. The path itself lists neither caller versions nor a new migration path, so it cannot alone determine the replacement scope.

## Boolean Track: Document One Read Completely

The Boolean track no longer uses correct Boolean values as its completion criterion. Every caller still using the fast read should leave a sequential-read record:

```text
Caller entry:
Caller version:
Pre-upgrade call pattern:
Original input:
Position before read:
Boolean result:
Adjacent field result:
Position after read:
Post-upgrade call pattern:
```

The order of the record has a practical purpose. Record the entry and version first so it is clear which usage this observation belongs to; then use the same input set to capture the position before the read, the Boolean result, the adjacent field, and the position after the read, so value changes can be separated from position changes. Only then place the pre-upgrade and post-upgrade call patterns side by side. Do not merge different callers into one conclusion that they are "verified," because one caller's byte layout cannot explain the subsequent fields for another caller.

If the Boolean result changes, retain the input and return to the Boolean-read segment, first confirming the read operation itself and the position before the read. If the Boolean result stays unchanged while the adjacent field changes, prioritize checking the read end position; this phenomenon cannot be recast as a table clear regression. If the positions before and after the read are also identical while the adjacent field still differs, this page can only record this combination; it cannot supply an unregistered call path as the cause.

Some records will reach only the entry. If a caller is found but its version cannot be confirmed, do not enter it into a replacement batch; the version is part of this migration record, not a note that can be filled in after replacement is complete. Conversely, knowing a version without having a verifiable entry is not enough to infer that it still uses the fast read.

Batch here means only a scope in which one confirmed caller is handled at a time. The existing materials provide no batch number, completed count, or specific replacement commit, so do not describe locating a file as meaning that a batch of callers has already been migrated.

## Corrections Left by the Review

The historical actions of SDK-209 preserve the Boolean track's timeline: 2025-10-13 moved from To Do to In Progress, and 2025-10-15 moved to In Review. The latter status indicates that the identified location and verification have been submitted for checking; it does not mean that every usage pattern has a result. The earlier wording that treated "entered review" as "caller covered" no longer applies.

Therefore, during review, keep the pre-upgrade input and result for the same caller together, and save different callers separately. One caller, Fang Ke, may only expose a misalignment in subsequent fields, while another may still be stuck with its version unconfirmed; both states are real migration positions and must not overwrite each other.

When starting from the old entry point, first confirm whether the caller still uses the fast read, then fill in that caller's version. Only after both items are confirmed should you take a set of inputs for a sequential read. If a record contains only the Boolean value and no positions before and after the read, it can be used to flag a review, but not to decide whether to replace it.

## table clear: The Parameter Flow Must Not Borrow the Boolean Result

table clear uses a separate parameter-flow record. It starts with a cleanup call that still worked before the upgrade, not with the Boolean-read file:

```text
Pre-upgrade cleanup call:
Pre-upgrade bigint parameter:
Pre-upgrade cleanup result:
Post-upgrade cleanup call:
Post-upgrade bigint parameter:
Value received by the binding layer:
Post-upgrade cleanup result:
Old call used for recovery:
```

First retain the pre-upgrade call, parameter, and result so that there is a comparable object when a difference appears after the upgrade. Then record the bigint parameter actually passed after the upgrade and the value received by the binding layer, followed by the cleanup result. The parameter's representation, the value passed at the call site, the value obtained by the binding layer, and the final result are separate observation points; merging some of these fields into "ABI normal" loses the locations that need follow-up.

If a difference appears between the post-upgrade parameter and the binding-layer value, stop at the current replacement point; do not prematurely attribute the cleanup result change to a read or table-state issue. If the value received by the binding layer is comparable but the cleanup result differs, record only that difference; the current materials provide no new function name or complete call path, so no cause can be invented for it. If the pre-upgrade call itself can no longer produce its result again, save the existing parameters, caller version, and difference fields, and wait for a scenario in which the old call can be reached again.

The only public information left by SDK-226 in 2025-10-31 is the one sentence: "table clear Call Boundary still has one unconfirmed point." This turns table clear from a vague post-upgrade regression into a clearly incomplete parameter-flow record, but the sentence does not identify whether the gap is in the call parameter, the binding layer, or the cleanup result. The old draft's judgment that directly assigned it to the result layer has been withdrawn; the corresponding fields in the table remain blank until actual review can fill them.

The Boolean track already has a history of one localization and review, but this does not narrow the unconfirmed scope of SDK-226. The two tracks must preserve inputs and results in their respective records: the key comparison for the former is the positions before and after the read and the adjacent field, while the key comparison for the latter is the pre-upgrade and post-upgrade parameters, the binding-layer value, and the cleanup result.

## Stop Points Before and After Replacement

Before replacing a Boolean caller, first save the old call pattern and a set of raw inputs. After replacement, check the Boolean result, adjacent field, and read end position at the same time. If a change appears, do not overwrite the old record; the old call and input are the basis for comparing the consumption position again. If the entry or version is missing, stop processing the current caller and leave it at the locator item SDK-209.

table clear replacement is performed separately. First obtain the bigint parameter and cleanup result from the old call, then observe the parameter passed by the new call, the value received by the binding layer, and the final result. If any field differs, restore the retained old call for comparison. Recovery here is documented only through restoring the old call and obtaining the result again: the existing materials contain no recovery commit, so it cannot be described as an existing automatic rollback.

When both tracks need review at the same time, first complete the one whose entry and version can be confirmed. Do not use the record from the other track to fill a gap for the sake of synchronizing batches. In particular, do not use the location of `binary_reader.ts` to explain table clear binding evidence, and do not use a bigint cleanup result to determine whether Boolean read consumption is correct.

## Current Verification Entry Points

- Fast Boolean decoding: enter via the code associated with `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/binary_reader.ts` near `BinaryReader`, look back at callers still using the fast read, and fill in the entry, version, and sequential-read record.
- table clear: enter from the pre-upgrade cleanup call and bigint parameter, recording the post-upgrade parameter, the value received by the binding layer, and the cleanup result separately.
- SDK-209: retain pending items for the Boolean caller's location, version, and review records.
- SDK-226: retain the field finding that bigint ABI still has one unconfirmed point.
- DOC-23: navigation for the adjacent validation design; this page does not merge its Range scan or cache hydration observations into these two migration tracks.

# Proposal to Separate Column Names from Accessors

Start with one assumption on the query.ts side: a database column name should not automatically be treated as the accessor exposed to callers on the TypeScript side. We don't yet have enough material to define the relationship between the two as an implementation rule, but if we keep treating them as the same name, later accessor changes will bring database-field compatibility concerns along with them.

Try two approaches first.

- Keep the database names used in queries separately retrievable, with accessors serving only as the names exposed on the SDK surface.
- Conversely, use the accessor as the sole name, then recover the database column name where queries need to be generated.

The initial draft favors the first approach. Not because it has been validated, but because the column name is what the query side needs to pass through consistently; changes to accessor names should not rewrite it by default. Keep the initial changes close to query modeling in query.ts, without using ConnectionId, Identity, or the index-type imports in the same file to expand the scope.

Counterexample needed: can the same column have both a public accessor and a database name? If that never happens, separating them would only add a useless mapping layer.

# Proposal to Separate Column Names from Accessors

The first review showed that the original assessment—"keeping two strings is enough"—was too simplistic. The query side doesn't just display names: calling Fang Ke lets you build conditions through accessors, while the generated column references need database names. If these two objects are pieced back together along the way, separation is still being deferred to the point where it is easiest to overlook.

The recommendation is now to narrow the experiment to where query objects get their names. One candidate approach is to store the database column name in the column metadata and retain the accessor where it needs to be exposed to TypeScript callers; QueryBuilder would take the name used for queries. The cost is that code building conditions must be explicit about which name it is using; it can no longer rely on property names happening to match.

Another candidate is to look up the mapping on the fly before rendering SQL. This involves fewer surface-level changes, but errors would only appear at the rendering stage; without a mapping, it would also require guessing whether the accessor can be used directly as a column name. It is therefore not the first choice for this round.

The initial draft also listed "all accessors should be renamed" as a possible migration path; that has now been removed. This is not about requiring existing API to be renamed, but about allowing existing database column names and accessors to differ. The first priority during migration should be to keep old accessors working; new mappings should not force existing queries to be rewritten.

Focus the review on crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/query.ts: confirm how query objects obtain column-related information before deciding whether the mapping belongs closer to the column metadata or the builder. The IndexColumns, IndexOpts, and ColumnIndex visible in the file show that index types and query objects are adjacent, but they are not alternative sources for these naming rules.

Still unconfirmed: whether columns without accessors should have default behavior; whether matching accessor and column names need special handling; whether to reject at the construction stage when a mapping is missing or keep the old pass-through path.

versions.body:
# Proposal for separating column names from accessors

This round brings the discussion back to query modeling, rather than using filenames to infer the scope of changes. The goal is to let database column names and TypeScript accessors exist independently, without forcing existing callers through an unrelated renaming migration. SDK-212 records the outcome of separating the two names while retaining existing calls; it provides a reference point, but does not replace the trade-offs discussed here.

The earlier draft described the problem as "keeping two strings." That is not enough: unless each name has its own place of use, the two will still end up being mixed up before query construction or rendering. The revised position is that the database column name should be retained with the column's metadata, while the accessor should remain part of SDK's caller-facing access model. Every path that needs to generate a column reference uses the database column name; every path that needs to organize calls by object property uses the accessor. It is common for the two to match, but the implementation cannot assume they do.

## Scope of this round's trial

The trial starts near the query objects in `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/query.ts`. That file already has type dependencies on `ColumnIndex`, `IndexColumns`, `IndexOpts`, and `UntypedSchemaDef`, indicating that column, index, and schema information meet here; this round only addresses where names come from. It does not change index semantics or treat the imports of `ConnectionId` or `Identity` as migration targets.

The proposed first step is to explicitly obtain the column names needed in query expressions from column metadata. The accessor can still serve as the access name when higher layers build conditions, but it should not be treated as an implicit stand-in for the database column name. This means tables where the names match incur no extra cost for callers, while tables where they differ will not rely on a later string replacement to work by chance.

"Explicitly obtain" does not mean adding a new set of public fields. First check whether the existing column metadata already carries both concepts; if it does, only clarify how they are passed through. If not, assess the smallest suitable place to hold them. Checking the former first avoids turning a compatibility fix into a reshaping of the schema surface.

## Options reviewed

**Look up the mapping before SQL rendering.** This is closest to the old behavior and keeps changes localized, but pushes naming errors to the very end. The renderer has to handle "which name to guess when no mapping is found," and diagnostics will also be far from where the accessor was actually chosen. Not prioritized this round.

**Treat the accessor as the sole authoritative name.** This would make the TypeScript surface tidier, but would require every database column reference to depend on rules for recovering the column name. It would also tie the stability of existing database field names to SDK property naming, which runs counter to the purpose of this separation.

**Keep column names in column metadata and accessors on the caller-facing surface.** This is the plan. The cost is that query objects need to deliberately choose which name to use, and tests need to cover cases where the two differ; the benefit is that errors stay closer to the modeling point, and old accessors can continue to serve existing calls.

The first two versions did not clearly explain one counterexample: if every accessor happens to match its database column name, all three approaches will appear to work. Verification cannot rely only on cases like these. We need to specifically find columns with differing names and observe which of the two names is actually used after conditions are built; if the current public entry point returns a result or throws an exception, record only what actually happens, not expectations written up as facts.

## Migration and rollback

The migration is not intended to "change the old accessors." Existing accessors remain in place, and any added or retained column-name information is used only to select the correct name on the query side. Callers should not rewrite object properties for this separation; if an existing call is found to already use database column names for direct access, first record it as a compatibility case, then decide whether an explicit mapping is needed.

The rollback conditions are narrowed accordingly: if column metadata cannot provide stable database column names, or if integrating it would change the behavior of existing queries where the names match, stop passing that mapping into query construction and restore the original way of passing names. Rolling back does not drop the confirmed requirement to distinguish the two names; it just avoids shipping an unverified choice of where to hold them.

The TODO in SDK-212 requires running through the public entry point and recording what is returned or thrown. This round should use it to distinguish two groups of cases: existing calls where the names match, and calls where the database column name differs from the accessor. The former checks compatibility; the latter checks whether the approach actually crosses the name boundary. Neither group can be considered complete just because type checking passes.

Three points remain to be confirmed: whether direct use of the column name is allowed when an accessor is missing; whether metadata with the same name but different origins needs to retain its provenance; and whether a missing mapping should trigger rejection during query construction or pass-through behavior should be retained temporarily. The last point particularly affects the rollback path; no decision on it will be made until the shape of the existing column metadata in query.ts is confirmed.

# HTTP Header Pass-Through Decision Record

The original draft treated HTTP header materialization and response pass-through as a single local decision, recorded near `crates/bindings-typescript/src/server/http_internal.ts`. This was not an interface constraint but an implementation trade-off within the compatibility train: introduce as few intermediate representations as possible, avoid making callers repeat header conversions, and check the status and body in the same review pass.

The decision made at the time should remain in the record. It explains why early investigations always landed on this file first, and why headers, status, and byte handling were included in the same set of questions.

| Approach | Assessment at the time | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Materialize headers as a list first, then reinterpret them during response construction | Conversion rules would live in two places, requiring back-and-forth comparison during review | Not selected |
| Store the intermediate representation in `Headers`, and use `headersToList` at the exit point | Both representations were already visible in the file; combining their handling first would make review easier | Adopted |

The direct dependencies visible at the time were:

```ts
import { Headers, headersToList } from 'headers-polyfill';
import status from 'statuses';
import BinaryReader from '../lib/binary_reader';
import BinaryWriter from '../lib/binary_writer';
```

The old decision treated the first two header names as an incoming/outgoing pair. The sketch below is retained from the record at the time; it shows the proposed handling, not a verified call chain.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Headers" as HeadersState
    state "headersToList" as HeaderListState
    [*] --> HeadersState
    HeadersState --> HeaderListState
    HeaderListState --> [*]
```

The rationale for adopting this approach was narrow: `headers-polyfill` already provided `Headers` and `headersToList`, so reusing them was considered more appropriate at the time than adding another layer of conversion objects nearby. The presence of `status`, `BinaryReader`, and `BinaryWriter` together reinforced the judgment that the response's status, headers, and body could be reviewed as consecutive boundaries. The draft therefore stated, "Callers don't need to know the intermediate form of the headers."

After review, that judgment needs to be revised, but the old paragraphs must not be deleted. The imports at the top of the file show only that the module depends on a header polyfill, status-related functionality, and binary read/write utilities; their presence together does not show that all objects flow in the same direction. The name `headersToList` does not prove that every type of response leaves through the same exit point, either. The original draft jumped directly from "visible in the same file" to "the same conversion boundary," with no actual references to support that step.

The original claim was stronger: **Requests and responses can share the same header materialization rules.** This is no longer suitable as an implementation conclusion. It remains here because subsequent review started from that assumption, not because an opposing design decision has already been reached.

The old decision has not been replaced with "Requests and responses must be kept separate." That would also go beyond what the existing record supports. The following questions remain unanswered in this review:

- whether `Headers` serves only one direction, or both requests and responses pass through it;
- whether the output of `headersToList` needs to preserve duplicate fields or input order;
- whether `status` is used for response object construction, error handling, or text conversion;
- whether `BinaryReader` and `BinaryWriter` cross the header boundary to handle the body.

Another reason for the old approach was convenience: concentrating changes within the compatibility train in one place would make differences easier to find. That reason still explains why it was adopted then, but it does not establish transport semantics. The retained working arrangement is simply not to have each caller duplicate header conversion; what has been withdrawn is the interpretation that "these callers necessarily share the same response pass-through path."

This page can therefore still serve as an entry point for the old investigation. If headers come up again, first check the actual use sites of `Headers` and `headersToList`, then determine whether status or binary objects belong in the same change. This page does not record enough reference findings to make a new decision.

# Identity Fixed-Width Proposal

The first draft treated fixed width as a change to a conversion function. `crates/bindings-typescript/src/lib/identity.ts` was right next to `AlgebraicType` and several U256 utility imports, so the working assumption at the time was that putting checks at this file's string entry point would be enough to handle the interface issue. That assumption is retained because it explains why early discussions leaned toward changing the entry point; it also mistook proximity within the file for the full compatibility boundary.

The two options listed in the earlier draft remain: add documentation only, or tighten validation at the entry point. The former leaves existing conversions uninterrupted; the latter centralizes the rules. The first draft had no examples and no caller version information, so "short values will be accepted" was only a suspected risk, not reproduced behavior. In particular, parameters, return values, or error behavior cannot be inferred directly from the names `fromstring` and `tohexstring`.

## Breakdown after this review

The interface review did not provide a fixed width that could be put straight into code, but it did break down the original problem. When a string enters Identity, the question is whether the input's length and representation are accepted by the interface; when Identity is converted back to a string, the question is whether the output consistently represents the same internal value. Handling only output leaves ambiguity on the input side; restricting only input may also cause existing values to come back as different text after a round trip.

These dependencies are still visible at the top of the file:

```ts
import { AlgebraicType } from './algebraic_type';
import { hexStringToU256, u256ToHexString, u256ToUint8Array } from './util';
```

They are enough to show that Identity sits alongside type descriptions and hexadecimal and U256 conversions, but they do not answer whether fixed width is defined in util, Identity, or a caller further out. The early draft skipped over this question. Leaving that gap explicit is more useful than turning import relationships into an implementation conclusion.

The review was not about "all text must immediately be the same length," but about what rules are needed at each of three points:

- On input, specify which string forms can still be passed for conversion and, if a length check exists, whether it happens before or after entering Identity.
- Internally, confirm whether the numeric representation inherently carries a width; if it is merely a temporary form used by a conversion utility, it should not be presented as a public format.
- On output, confirm whether `tohexstring` makes a fixed-width commitment. If it does, leading characters and letter case can no longer be left for callers to guess.
- For round trips, first decide what to compare: whether numeric values match, or whether the text must also stay the same. These two requirements lead to different compatibility handling.

These points remain review notes, not a published interface specification. The earlier draft's proposal for "centralized checks at the entry point" is now treated as a candidate rather than the default decision.

## Options

**A: Add interface documentation only.**

Treat fixed width as an existing but insufficiently documented convention, without changing the conversion path. The advantage is that this does not change when existing callers fail. The problem is that if the existing conversion actually allows text of different lengths, documentation cannot replace validation. This option requires first finding callers that use Identity's string entry point; no such material is available, so A remains only a low-cost option and cannot support a claim that compatibility has been established.

**B: Normalize at the entry point.**

Check and normalize text where Identity receives a string, then pass it to the existing conversion utility. This allows input and output tests to be written separately and failures to surface earlier. The cost is that an existing caller Fang Ke may go from getting an internal value to failing at the entry point; if fixed width is actually only an internal representation requirement, this would wrongly push an internal restriction out to the external interface. The early draft leaned toward this option; that preference is no longer treated as a conclusion.

**C: Compatible reads, fixed output.**

Temporarily retain existing input forms and emit only one fixed form on output, pending caller migration. This avoids cutting off old inputs all at once, but multiple input texts will coexist during the compatibility period. Debugging requires knowing which form was passed in; otherwise, "the output changed" does not tell us whether the cause is conversion behavior or the caller's existing data. There is no material available to support a decision on whether additional logging for this is worthwhile.

The three options differ not over whether util can perform the conversion, but over when the text format is treated as a public commitment. If fixed width is later confirmed to serve only internal objects, neither B nor C should cross the interface boundary; A can only record that assessment, not present it as a format guarantee to callers.

## Experiments: start with counterexamples

If B or C moves forward, the minimal example set should not contain just a single normal Identity value. At a minimum, put side by side an input of the proposed width, an input that is too short, an input that is too long, and an input whose text changes after one round trip. Whether to retain leading characters and whether to normalize hexadecimal letter case are both choices that affect text comparisons.

The experiments also need to distinguish where failure occurs. If the underlying conversion rejects a value before the length check, that result only shows that a deeper layer does not accept that input; it does not prove that the entry point has enforced the fixed-width rule. Conversely, if conversion succeeds but output length is unstable, changing only the output function is not enough to explain the input-side compatibility semantics. Records should include the original text, the names of the functions it passed through, and the returned text; "pass" or "fail" alone is insufficient for later comparison.

There is no specific width, case rule, or failure output here, so we won't make up numbers or error messages. The early proposal left these as implementation details; the review suggests that at least some of them will be part of the interface decision.

## Migration assessment and rollback points

Before adopting B, first confirm what forms callers that still use the string entry point actually store and pass in. If entry-point validation prevents existing callers from creating an Identity, roll back that validation first, retain the original conversion path, and then decide whether callers should handle the format migration. When adopting C, if the same internal value produces unpredictable text at different points because of different legacy inputs, roll back the combination of "compatible reads, fixed output" rather than just temporarily relaxing a particular length condition.

SDK-217 is retained as a navigation aid for this investigation. It calls for adding an example from a caller still using fixed-width compatibility and verifying the actual version, entry point, and result. Until that example is available, A, B, and C all remain candidates; this page preserves the trade-offs and rollback conditions from that time, not a final description of Identity's current format.

# Caller Dual-State Incident Postmortem

During caller integration testing, the same object returned different current revisions at two points in time. At the first check, `moduleHooks` did not match the old record; a later check using the original input still confirmed only the current entry point. There were not enough records between the two results to explain the change, so the later result was not used to overwrite the original record.

## Timeline

- After the discrepancy was found, the record from that time was retained and further retries were stopped. Repeated reads could only return a new current state, not recover the request context from the first read.
- The version, request context, and stop conditions were added at handoff. The original record and recovery page were saved separately to avoid mistaking the recovery result for the initial observation.
- Subsequent checks confirmed that `DecompressionStream` could be restored. This showed only that the recovery action was usable, not that the object's state had stabilized.
- The change in `HttpResponse` remained unexplained. Retracing the path with the original input during verification did not reproduce all branches either; the unreproduced parts were kept as open investigation items.

## Impact Scope

The affected areas were the real-world call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback built up around sdks. When the same object shows different states at different times, the caller Fang Ke may treat an old record as the current revision and may also mistake a successful result after a single recovery for full recovery. The existing records did not identify adjacent services as the cause, and were not used to conclude that all call samples were affected.

## Retained State

`docs/adj-sdks/incidents/sdks-caller-integration-same-object-two-states.md` retains the initial observation, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause. This project has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria; this anomaly did not change the exit action, and only the state at the point retries were stopped was retained. The window doesn't start with the four Chinese characters for "Release successful," nor does it end when you see one green result. Preserve the last visible result before handling exit actions. Verify the exit action for adj-sdks independently; the relevant owner must still sign off separately on whether the release succeeded.

## Preserve the original state first

- [ ] Open the current entry point from `docs/adj-sdks/release/sdks-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md` and record the version, time, and first result shown on the page.
- [ ] Find `databaseIdentity`, then check `messageQueue`. Finding only the former isn't enough to close the window; if you see `messageQueue`, don't clear the state.
- [ ] Check whether `useTable` is present. If it's missing, stop further exit actions and retain the absence itself as a result.

v1 made "don't clear the state after seeing `messageQueue`" a separate stop point. At the time, there were no recovery records in the shared environment yet, so that version retained only TODO. That decision still applies to preserving the originals, but it didn't specify where to cross-check after the page's entry point changes.

## Checks when closing the window

1. Keep one sample each of the project's own success path and a rejection path. Use the samples only to confirm the last visible result; don't substitute "success" in the logs for the page or object state.
2. Verify the artifacts or state for `QueryBuilder`, then decide whether to complete the exit action. Seeing that the call has returned doesn't mean the exit action has completed.
3. Check whether the queue is still accepting new work. If new work is still coming in, stop closing the window; don't hide it with cleanup.
4. Before removing the temporary bypass, confirm that doing so won't overwrite the original failure window. If you won't be able to retrieve the original result after removing it, stop before proceeding.

The records from SDKA-001 later noted that the expiry action was no longer valid, but the entry-point hint on the page had not yet been updated. So "can be reviewed via the current entry point" can't just mean that the link opens; also check whether the entry-point hint still points to this window. The reproduction records from SDKA-005 also documented missing intermediate records. When an intermediate window is missing, align `sdks-client-integration` with the current entry point, leave the gaps blank, and don't directly subtract the two results on either side of the gap.

## When you can't proceed

- `useTable` is missing: stop; do not perform recovery.
- Can't find the original final result: stop; don't substitute a cleaned-up copy.
- The queue is still accepting new work: stop closing the window; preserve the window object first.

If recovery results appear later, append them to this checklist; don't overwrite the original failure window. This is how the entry point for SDKA-012 was used.

# Caller Exit Window Checklist

Before closing the window, answer one narrow question: does the exit action for adj-sdks already have a last visible result? This is not the same as whether the overall release succeeded. The release result still requires separate sign-off from the relevant owner; this page only keeps the objects, exit actions, and results from the window that can be revisited.

## Check sequence

Start from `docs/adj-sdks/release/sdks-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`, not from the consolidated results page. The entry-point hint may not have changed along with the expiry action, an issue that was left unresolved later. Once you open it, first record the version and time currently displayed, then find these three objects:

- `databaseIdentity`: confirm that you are looking at the object for this window.
- `messageQueue`: confirm whether the window may still receive new work.
- `useTable`: use it as one signal from the live state for proceeding with the exit action.

The old wording was "Find `databaseIdentity`; after you see `messageQueue`, do not clear the state; stop if `useTable` has not appeared." This passage has not been deleted because it accurately preserves how earlier windows were handled. However, it does not cover an outdated entry-point hint or explain how recovery results should sit alongside failure results. Do not treat the old paragraph as new release policy.

## Open the window

1. [ ] Follow the current entry point to find `databaseIdentity`, and put the object value, the version displayed on the page, and the first visible result in a single record.
2. [ ] Check whether `messageQueue` is still receiving new work. As long as the queue is still changing, pause the exit action. Do not clear the state, delete the original results, or use "the queue is empty" to infer prior success.
3. [ ] Check `useTable`. If you cannot find it, stop at the current window and save "has not appeared" as the result. Do not proceed directly to recovery or fill the gap with a result of the same name from another object.
4. [ ] Check against one sample of the project's own success path and one of its rejection path. Use the two samples only to identify the last visible result; they cannot replace the values from the original window.

"Last" here means the result that can still be seen from the original entry point before the exit action. It is not a green summary compiled afterward, nor a success line in the logs without object context. If the entry point opens but there is no record for the intervening window, preserve that gap; the earlier and later results cannot be subtracted directly. The situation recorded in SDKA-001—"the expiry action is no longer valid, but the page's entry-point hint has not been updated"—is exactly this case: an existing link does not mean the hint reflects the current window.

## Stop points for closing the window

Handle the following actions in order. Stop if any item has no result:

- [ ] The artifact or status for `QueryBuilder` has been inspected and matched to this window's object; seeing only the call return does not complete the check.
- [ ] The last visible result can still be revisited through the entry point and has not been overwritten during temporary reorganization.
- [ ] The queue is no longer receiving new work, or it is still receiving work but window closure has explicitly been halted.
- [ ] Temporary bypasses that need to be removed have been listed. If removal could change the live state, do not remove them yet; preserve the original window.

"The project team will continue to monitor" is no substitute for an actual person taking over. The handoff record should state which action is unfinished and what was last visible. If no one can confirm yet, leave the status unconfirmed rather than changing it to release failure or release success. Stop when you go beyond the scope of objects the adj-sdks page can confirm; the release decision goes back to the relevant owner.

## Failure and recovery

`databaseIdentity` cannot be found: stop. First confirm the entry point and object; do not clear the window.

`messageQueue` is still changing: stop closing the window. Do not perform cleanup that would make results disappear.

`useTable` has not appeared: stop recovery and preserve the current page and the missing-object state.

The final result cannot be found, or only a consolidated copy is available: stop. Do not overwrite the original record with the copy. The rule in SDKA-009 is to check both the current entry point and the original current revision; if both are missing, leave the status unknown. Unknown here does not mean zero results.

If recovery later produces a result, append it to `sdks-client-integration Exit Window Checklist` and keep it alongside the original failed window. The explicit requirement in SDKA-012 is not to overwrite the original failed window or object. The recovery result can show what was seen after this action, but it cannot be written back as though the earlier window had succeeded all along.

## Old traces left on the page

v1 had only the entry point, three objects, and the "recovery has not yet been tried in the shared environment" TODO. v2 added the rejection path, the `QueryBuilder` check, and handling for missing intermediate records; the outdated entry-point hint also remained an issue. Later additions can include more samples, but do not use new samples to fill gaps in earlier windows. The adjacent DOC-34 documents a route that was not adopted; this page does not decide on a solution for it.

# Compatibility Directory Dual-State Incident Postmortem

When this issue was first seen, `messageQueue` did not match the old record. The same entry point returned different current revisions at two points in time, so the status shown on the page could not be treated as the same record. This concerns the public contract formed around the schema and the impact of migration records on caller compatibility; this directory has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, so a single entry-point discrepancy cannot be generalized directly into a status change for the entire project.

## Sequence of Events

- First, we preserved the content of `docs/adj-templates/incidents/templates-compatibility-catalog-same-object-two-states.md` as it was at the time; the later page was not used to overwrite the original record. The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause were kept separately.
- We then stopped retrying. Retrying would only continue changing the observed state and could not show which of the two states should be adopted.
- After clearing our own cache, we reran it once, leaving the shared cache untouched at first. This was to check whether local residue could still affect reads through the entry point; at the time, this was not recorded as a proven root cause.
- During the review, the only additional observation was the one at `Timestamp`. The other branches did not reproduce the issue, and missing points in time were not filled in with speculation.

## Observed Results

`useTable` can be restored. This recovery only shows that the entry point returned to an available state on rerun; it cannot explain why the revisions before and after differed. There is still no explanation for the change in `subscriptionBuilder`, and the original record also lacked enough evidence to tie it to any one of the following: the cache, migration records, or caller compatibility. So at the time, both states were kept as originally recorded rather than selecting one state and making it the sole conclusion.

The on-call handoff added the version, request context, and stop conditions to avoid looking only at the final green line of output. Unconfirmed timeline points include what happened before the discrepancy first appeared and whether the same entry point would still return another current revision after recovery. If the investigation continues, `templates-compatibility-catalog`, the current entry point, and the command should be held constant, with only the current revision replaced; this path comes from the pending investigation record from that time and has not been adopted as this page's closure conclusion.

This export remains in `adj-templates`, under `incident-export`. The page can navigate back to the original record and recovery page, but the old assessment here applies only to the state of the incident at that time; it was not consolidated into the directory status description currently in use.
