# Package Integration Blocker Troubleshooting Tree

When demo-package-integration appears stuck at the current entry point, first preserve the original symptom in the record, then decide whether to investigate within the project, exit, or hand off to the permissions owner. Here, "stuck" is not a root-cause name: the same symptom may result from input not being collected, an inconsistent entry point and environment, a problem with the project's own resources, or a difference that only appears at a cross-package boundary.

```text
Current entry point
├─ No original record
│  └─ Collect first; do not proceed to root-cause assessment
└─ Has original record
   └─ Compare the first difference with the most recent normal QueryBuilder sample
      ├─ No difference
      │  └─ Check the entry point or environment; stop if there is still no new evidence
      └─ Has difference
         ├─ Still within demo-package-integration
         │  └─ Investigate along the in-project branch; do not hand off to the shared owner first
         └─ A clear interface has been crossed
            └─ Preserve the sample, then hand off to the corresponding owner
```

## What to save first

At a minimum, preserve the first visible result, the raw input, the version used at the time, and snippets that can show environmental differences. A green result from a rerun cannot overwrite the first failure; it can only show that the later run did not reproduce the same symptom. Directory names, averages, and the final display can all help with locating the issue, but they cannot replace intermediate records.

Change only one condition during a single investigation. Do not change QueryBuilder, the entry point, and the environment at the same time; otherwise, even if the symptom disappears, it will be impossible to know which change produced the result. When there is no original record, the tree stops at "collect first." Without evidence, do not jump directly from a field name to an exit action.

## When these terms appear in records

Older records treated several implementation terms as nodes in the tree: `useProcedure`, `Timestamp`, `BooleanExpr`, `databaseIdentity`, `Bound`, `Range`, `outgoingMessages`, `messageQueue`, `microsSinceUnixEpoch`, `BinaryWriter`, `ResizableBuffer`, `columnMetadata` and `useTable`. They are points in the evidence where investigation can continue, not standalone root-cause categories. When you see one of these terms, record only which segment of the input, output, or call trace it appears in; if there is no second sample, do not infer behavior from the name.

Earlier wording used `Timestamp` as a reminder before cleaning up the evidence, and `BooleanExpr` as the stopping point when there was no further material. This layer is still retained because it helps with reviewing old records, but it does not indicate that the recovery action has been verified in the shared environment. Samples added later also left `useTable`, `Bound` and `Range` beside different nodes; for now, they can only be treated as labels that need to be compared, not arranged into an unconfirmed call chain.

`microsSinceUnixEpoch` was once added as a local observation that the project had already seen. It may indicate that the time representation needs to be rechecked, but it cannot by itself prove that the time difference caused the blockage. The same applies to `BinaryWriter`, `ResizableBuffer` and `columnMetadata`: if one appears only in a single failure record, stop at that record; do not expand it into a complete explanation involving serialization, buffers, or column metadata.

## Branch One: No Sample, or Sample Not at the Same Entry Point

If the current entry point has no original record, first add a record of the input seen at failure and the first output. Do not fill the gap with a successful result from a rerun. If all you have is the final page, a directory name, or a description saying "stuck," the branch stops at collection; at this point, you cannot determine whether demo-package-integration itself is the problem.

If there is a record but it cannot be aligned with the most recent normal QueryBuilder sample, first check the entry point and environment. Keep the original text from both sides during the comparison; do not copy only the conclusion after the difference. Different versions, inputs, or resource permissions can only be treated as differences to verify; without a second piece of local evidence, do not choose one of them as the cause.

Older versions once recommended retrying promptly after seeing the symptom. That handling did not retain enough of the first failure sample, so now treat retrying only as a supplementary observation. Retrying and getting the same symptom can add a clue; retrying and getting a different symptom also cannot erase the original record. Cleaning up the evidence will make the tree lose its basis for branching.

## Branch Two: The Difference Remains Within the Project

When the first difference still falls within demo-package-integration's own resource, permission, or index scope, continue through the in-project records. Here you can check whether the corresponding input exists, whether the output was produced from the same entry point, and whether the in-project version combination matches the normal sample. Stop at the first point that requires new material; there is no need to keep guessing merely to obtain a terminal term.

If the record shows permission denied, first distinguish the permissions for the entry point currently being used from the permissions for the detail object. The entry point being open does not mean that the detail object can also be read; the detail object being readable does not mean that the resources required for package integration are available. If the material shows only one of these layers, preserve the result for that layer and leave the other as unknown. The condition for handing off to the permissions owner is that the issue has actually exceeded the range that can be handled within the project.

If the record shows only a node name, with no corresponding input, output, or call snippet, do not treat the node name as a failure action. For example, if `useProcedure` is not followed by a result, that means the tree lacks evidence here; it does not mean that procedure itself failed. When `useTable` appears only on the input side, you also cannot infer that the downstream has already consumed that table.

## Branch Three: The Difference Crosses an Interface

If the first difference no longer belongs to demo-package-integration, but appears at a clear cross-package interface, first put the confirmed in-project portion together with the raw fragment at the interface, then hand it off to the corresponding owner. The handoff content only carries the evidence; it does not decide the root cause on the other party's behalf. If the interface boundary itself has no sample, the tree stops at the boundary; do not fill it in with the name of a neighboring project.

SDKC-010 were once used to split the source and adopter for the two current entry points. A later card record stated that this was merged into the maintenance card for the same module, and the earlier claim that mistakenly treated the on-duty person as the adoption status is also void. This change explains why the old path can still be found, but the old path should not be treated as a new responsibility mapping. SDKC-013 recorded the cleanup scope for obsolete entry-point navigation; the original record and date can still be reviewed, but the current page treats them only as navigation context.

When handing off across packages, state at least: the last node confirmed within demo-package-integration, the name of the interface crossed, the first failed output, and whether a recent normal sample exists. If any item is missing, state the missing item and stop at the current branch point. Do not use "looks like" as a substitute for interface evidence, and do not conflate the permissions owner, package maintainer, and adopter into a single role.

## Old Wording and Current Stopping Points

The old draft directly treated "no `BooleanExpr`" as a stopping condition, and also associated "seeing `Timestamp`" with cleaning up the evidence. These statements remain in the historical records, but they can only express the troubleshooting habits at the time. The current branch stops based on which new piece of evidence is missing, not on whether a particular term appears.

The old draft also left `databaseIdentity` at the edge of the evidence, and scattered `Bound`, `Range`, `outgoingMessages` and `messageQueue` across different positions in the tree. They were not merged into a single unified conclusion. When reviewing, first confirm the direction in which the term appeared: input, output, log, or code path; if the direction is unclear, retain only the original fragment.

If the symptom changes midway through the investigation, open a new local record and note the samples before and after the change. Do not use a later success to overwrite an earlier failure, and do not splice results from two different environments into a single timeline. If it is only a project-internal resource or permission issue, it can be wrapped up within demo · Package Integration Collaboration; if changing the user-visible behavior of a shared interface is required, stop this page's tree and move to formal review.

## Entry Point Still Retained

`docs/adj-demo/runbooks/demo-package-integration-who-to-handoff-to-when-blocked.md` remains the lookup entry for this group of adj-demo records. SDKC-010 and SDKC-013 are used only to find related source splits and obsolete navigation records; this does not mean that this page has made new maintenance decisions for them. Future implementation, shared-environment recovery actions that have not yet been tried, and nodes without support from original samples all remain at the tree's stopping point.

# Quality Signal Entry Point Migration Procedure

This page records the entry point migration for sqltest · Quality Signal Board. The scope is failure samples, regression tiering, and flaky-signal attribution built around test and spec. Record old entry points, new entry points, and compatibility callers separately; don't judge only by whether a new name appears in the directory.

## The Two Options Seen at the Time

Earlier records compared `Timestamp` and `BooleanExpr`. The preference left in the record is to split `BooleanExpr` out on its own: the two parts have different failure exit points, and continuing to use `Timestamp` would mix different types of failures into the same entry point. This was only the assessment at the time; it cannot be taken as proof that all callers have completed the switch.

`columnMetadata` is the new entry-point object observed in this migration. It should be recorded together with its actual consumers; don't automatically include side paths with similar names. The active callers for `BinaryReader` had not been determined at the time, so this remains a gap in the old record and must not be marked complete in the migration results.

## Migration Sequence

1. First, list the callers still using the old entry point and record the type of failure sample each depends on and whether its results fall under regression tiering or flaky-signal attribution.
2. Then point each caller to the current entry point, retaining the old entry-point name and compatibility location. Change only the index target; don't delete the old documentation first.
3. Check the failure exit points against actual test and spec results. A new entry point appearing in the directory, a filename change, or a single successful run is not enough to show that the caller's migration is complete.
4. Have the actual consumer confirm the switch results, then update the status of that row. If no consumer has been found, retain the search scope and an unconfirmed label; don't fill in an inferred conclusion.

During the migration, the independent schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria remain part of sqltest · Quality Signal Board's own records. Don't mix in schedules or maintenance arrangements from adjacent projects here.

## Switch Back to the Old Entry Point

If the failure exit points after the switch cannot be explained, or the caller has not yet confirmed the switch, first restore that caller's old entry point, then continue comparing the routing results for `Timestamp` and `BooleanExpr`. When restoring it, roll back only the entry-point target and retain the recorded `columnMetadata` observations; don't also mark the unconfirmed `BinaryReader` relationship as restored. Once the caller provides results again, update the migration row.

This index corresponds to `docs/adj-sqltest/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. Future maintenance should continue to use the entry points recorded in this file for verification; pages with similar names cannot fill in details about the actual state here. The old documentation and dates remain available for reference; the parts about the last consumers, side-path calls, and rollback scope were not fully resolved at the time and may still be out of date.

# Postmortem on the Two Versions of the Quality Signal Record

This page was originally placed next to the entry point to document the situation left behind when two identically named documents had not been merged. Later additions did not remove the old paragraphs, so the initial conjectures, the read paths that have recovered, and the questions that remain unanswered are all retained here.

The entry-point file is `docs/adj-sqltest/incidents/sqltest-quality-signal-board-two-version-records-not-merged.md`. It comes from incident-export in sqltest · Quality Signal Board, and that project still maintains the body and attachments. The initial anomaly was narrowly scoped: the `current revision` for two revisions appeared at the same entry point simultaneously. Readers could find them under the same name, but could not treat them as the same record.

The first round of comparison initially encountered `BooleanExpr`. At the time, there was no complete list of adopters, nor any material explaining at which stage the difference arose; after preserving the original input and the entry-point version, the responders stopped retrying with the same input. The old record stated that `BinaryReader` could recover, while why `Range` had changed was still unknown. These two statements remain here because they describe a recovery result and an unresolved question respectively, not a single cause.

The missing time points were not filled in later. The original record has no verifiable time points for when the impact began, how long the old revision remained at the entry point, or whether all attachments had been synchronized. Filling these gaps with a precise sequence would make this postmortem look more complete than what was observed at the time, so they remain unknown. There is also no list of adopters that can be filled in retroactively; seeing two versions of the material at the entry point is not enough to establish that every consumer read the old content.

## The Sequence at the Time

| Time point | What was observed at the time | Action taken during the incident | What could still be confirmed later |
|---|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `sqltest-Quality Signal Console-two record versions not merged` deviated from the baseline | Preserved the original input and the entry-point version | Two revisions had appeared at the same entry point |
| T+07 | `QueryBuilder` was still normal | Narrowed the scope of observation | The entire sqltest · Quality Signal Board could not be declared unavailable |
| T+18 | The comparison pointed to `BooleanExpr` | Preserved the object showing a difference | The difference was visible at least when comparing the two records |
| T+31 | The user path recovered | Recorded recovery and attribution separately | Path recovery did not mean the cause had been confirmed |

T+00 through T+31 are relative time points used during the incident, not a set of dates filled in afterward. The timeline is not a complete request log either; it only shows what was preserved first, which path later recovered, and which judgments were not validated by that recovery. In particular, the normal result at T+07 ruled out the overly broad description that "all query objects failed simultaneously," but did not identify where the two record versions had failed to merge.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Same entry point
    participant O as Old revision
    participant C as Current revision
    participant R as Incident record
    E->>O: Read the old record
    E->>C: Current record appears at the same time
    O-->>R: BooleanExpr difference
    C-->>R: User path recovers
```

The two read arrows in the diagram only reconstruct the side-by-side relationship at the entry-point layer. It is not an execution sequence diagram, nor does it indicate that the old revision was necessarily used before the current revision. What could be confirmed during the incident was that the same entry point could expose two records; the actual order in which the objects were called cannot be inferred from this diagram.

The initial attribution was later withdrawn. Someone had attributed the difference to the execution path solely because different records appeared under one entry point; however, `QueryBuilder` was still normal during the comparison, and the user path also recovered at T+31. This combination was insufficient to support the claim that "the execution path as a whole was broken." The old judgment was not deleted; a correction was added beside it: the problem manifested at least as two versions side by side at the record entry point, but attribution of why they had not merged was not completed during the incident.

This correction did not narrow the failure to a purely documentation-related issue. The two record versions at the entry point did cause the comparison results to diverge, and `BooleanExpr` was an object already observed at the time; however, the material did not establish that the divergence affected only presentation, nor that it had reached every read path. Therefore, starting with the second version, "versions side by side at the entry point," "differences in individual objects," and "user path recovery" were recorded separately rather than compressed into a single root cause.

Another secondhand account containing only screenshots did not resolve this gap either. It lacked an account, version, and run id, and could not explain why one path was normal while another deviated. Only in the later handoff were the version, request context, and stopping conditions added to the record: when an entry-point deviation is seen again, first preserve the input and both revisions; if all that is available is the last green result, do not state a definitive cause.

This does not mean screenshots are worthless. They can show that a particular result was observed, and can help locate the entry point used at the time; the problem is that they cannot replace a version comparison. Without the original input, it is impossible to determine whether the difference in `BooleanExpr` came from the two records; without request context, it is also impossible to assess a recovered path and another path that still deviates together.

There is an old conclusion here that is easy to misread: `BinaryReader` has recovered. It means that one local read path became available again, not that the two revisions had merged, nor that all adopters had read the same content. The reason for the change in `Range` is still unknown; the two cannot be linked into a proven causal chain merely because both appeared during this incident.

The recovery record also has a limited role. The user path became available again after T+31, which meant the person on duty no longer needed to treat the situation as "everything is unavailable"; it did not fill in the impact window or tell us when the old revision disappeared from the entry point. The gaps left in the first version still apply: what is missing is not a concluding statement, but the original time points needed to verify the start, duration, and scope of adoption.

Later test samples allowed the record to compare rendered results more concretely. One retained output was:

```sql
SELECT * FROM "person" WHERE "person"."active" = TRUE
```

It shows that the comparison of the Boolean predicate at the time had fixed SQL text; it did not replace the comparison of entry-point versions. This sample was used to confirm that the record content had not undergone another kind of change during rendering, not to prove that all objects had passed through the same read path.

Another equality-filter sample was retained as `createdAt = '2024-01-01T00:00:00.123000Z'`. It and the Boolean-predicate sample belong to the same round of retrospective review material: both help distinguish "the output text can still be compared" from "the two records have merged." The former can be seen in the samples; the latter cannot be inferred from a single SQL output.

A sample was later attached to SDKD-001, providing a navigation point for revisiting the input used at the time. That sample did not replace the version comparison between the two revisions, nor did it fill in the scope of consumers. Its only relevance to this anomaly is the need to confirm that the old edge has actually disappeared when retracting the old relationship; it cannot be used in reverse to prove that the entry-point layer has been unified.

DOC-43 can serve as a navigation point for the old entry-point migration index. This page preserves the situation during an anomaly in which two record versions appeared side by side. Both pages belong to sqltest · Quality Signal Board, but the names in the migration index are not a list of those affected by this anomaly, and the adopters appearing in the index cannot be directly counted as being within the scope of this deviation.

The old version once presented "putting the current revision for two revisions at the same entry point" as though it were a complete explanation. This statement is still retained, but must be understood within its original scope: it describes the structure observed during the incident, not where the merge operation failed. Subsequent comparisons confirmed that `QueryBuilder` had not deviated along with it, and also preserved the difference in `BooleanExpr`; these additions refute the overly broad attribution to the execution path, rather than fabricate a root cause to fill in the old record.

After recovery, the boundaries at the entry-point layer were somewhat clearer than in the first version: two revisions were exposed simultaneously by the same entry point; `QueryBuilder` was normal; at least one user path had recovered. Beyond those boundaries, gaps remain: the total number of affected adopters, how long the old revision was read, whether the change in `Range` was caused by the same point of divergence, and whether the attachments were synchronized along with the entry point. Where the old version had no evidence, the later additions did not turn the unknowns into definitive conclusions either.

### Retained Passages from the Original Record

> adj-sqltest once placed the `current revision` for two revisions at the same entry point; the old judgment, later findings, and still-unknown scope of adoption are presented side by side in chronological order.

This sentence is a condensed statement from the early record. It does not list the adopters, nor does it claim that the merge had been completed. It is retained because the response sequence at the time really did start with the versions appearing side by side at the entry point, rather than with an already confirmed internal cause.

> `BinaryReader` can recover, while why `Range` changed is still unknown.

This still describes the unresolved part of this page. What recovered was a local path; the cause of `Range` was not confirmed along with the recovery. Quoting only the first half would misrepresent the old incident as fully fixed; quoting only the second half would omit the scope that had already recovered at the time.

This does not mean the entry point has no compatibility risks; it only acknowledges that the material available at the time was not yet sufficient to support an irreversible change. The window can continue to be prepared, but it cannot take effect before the verification results for the public-facing entry point, contrasting inputs, and one replayable run are available.

Retain the old entry point as the rollback point. versions.body:
# Decision Record for Maintaining the Public Entry Point

The initial draft framed the choice as "keep the current query-model entry point, or adjust the cutover window". After review, this question remains, but it is no longer treated as a single action. Whether the entry point continues to handle existing calls is a public-interface decision; the window is a coordination arrangement. The two are related, but neither can replace the other.

The decisions for this round are as follows: retain query-model as the current public entry point; allow preparations to adjust the window to continue; do not approve using the window arrangement as a direct replacement for reviewing the entry point; keep the old entry point available as a rollback point if discrepancies arise. This scope is narrower than the initial draft. It covers only public behavior already observed and does not also treat unexamined query forms as having completed migration.

## Two Matters Separated During the Meeting

The first matter is where existing calls enter. Keeping the existing entry point lets calls already in use retain the same access point and gives the review results a stable reference point to revisit. The second matter is when the team expands the cutover scope. The window can help schedule preparation work, but it cannot prove that behavior after the adjustment remains the same as before.

The initial draft included a more optimistic interpretation: since the window could coordinate the cutover centrally, each integration point could handle entry-point differences on its own during migration. This interpretation was not adopted during review. Doing so would scatter differences that should have been visible at the public interface; the fact that a particular call has not reported a problem for the time being also cannot, conversely, establish that the entry point is compatible.

The window therefore records only coordination status and makes no compatibility determination. It can indicate that an adjustment is still in preparation, but it cannot label "in preparation" as "verified". For calls without replay results, this record makes no additional judgment and does not accept their migration results by default simply because they fall within the same window.

## Basis for the Decision

The meeting materials require every compatibility conclusion to be grounded in three things at once: the public entry point in the frozen revision, inputs that run counter to the behavior intended to be preserved, and a replayable run. These contrasting inputs are inputs sufficient to reveal whether the proposed change alters externally observable behavior, not just an arbitrary rerun of the same example.

This assessment method deliberately avoids tracing conclusions back to speculation about the implementation. Internal code that appears likely to preserve a particular behavior cannot, on its own, justify approving an expanded window; conversely, one successful local example cannot establish that all query constructs will remain unchanged. Only the portion supported by the materials is approved.

The frozen location continues to use the existing query reference in `crates/bindings-typescript/tests/query.test.ts`. It helps return to the public behavior examined at the time and does not mean that the file is permanently responsible for the public entry point. If later changes move the test layout elsewhere, the decision itself will still be based on public output and replayable results, not on whether the path remains unchanged.

## Two Reviewed Examples

When a Boolean column is used directly as a predicate, the saved rendered output is `SELECT * FROM "person" WHERE "person"."active" = TRUE`. This round treats that output as a concrete compatibility example supporting retention of the entry point. This is not merely a comparison of the general meaning of SQL: table-name qualification, column qualification, predicate position, and `TRUE` are all part of the textual result that has been reviewed. If the output's form changes after the adjustment, the conclusion for this example cannot simply be carried over, even if someone considers the semantics similar.

The replay example for a timestamp equality filter is `createdAt = '2024-01-01T00:00:00.123000Z'`. This record also pins down the column name, spaces on both sides of the equals sign, single quotes, and the UTC representation with six decimal places. It shows that the current entry point preserves the expected text for this particular input; it does not show that other comparison operators, other column names, or other time values have been checked.

These two examples support the limited decision that "the current entry point will continue serving existing calls". During the meeting, some interpreted the passing examples to mean that the window could be expanded immediately. After review, these two matters were separated: the text outputs already observed are reviewed evidence, while inputs not yet replayed remain only a scope awaiting confirmation. The former cannot fill the gaps in the latter.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Existing query-model entry point] --> B[Public behavior review]
    B --> C[Reviewed examples]
    C --> D[Keep current entry point]
    E[Adjust cutover window] --> F[Call scope in preparation]
    F --> B
    D --> G[Keep old entry point]
    G --> H[Roll back and reproduce when discrepancies arise]
```

The window in the diagram is not a substitute node for the entry point. It can only send the scope in preparation back for review; only reviewed behavior is included in this round's retention decision. The old entry point remains in place after the decision so that a comparison can be obtained again if discrepancies arise, rather than serving as a temporary decoration that automatically disappears when the window ends.

## Paths Compared

**Keep the current entry point.** This path lets existing calls continue to enter through the same public location. Its benefit is that reviewed outputs do not need to rely on the window description for explanation; discrepancies can also be reproduced by returning to the same entry point. The cost is equally clear: the team cannot complete all cutovers through a single entry-point change, and coordinators must continue to distinguish integrations under observation from integrations that are only planned.

This cost was accepted. Maintaining two paths adds coordination overhead for a period of time, but preserves an operational rollback point. By contrast, expanding the scope without sufficient behavioral evidence risks more than scheduling complexity: it may change the external boundaries of existing calls without leaving a clear place to establish where the change begins.

**Use the window to drive the entry-point cutover.** The appeal of this path is that it allows scheduling to be coordinated centrally at an earlier stage and reduces the perception of two coexisting sets of entry points. The objection is not that the window has no value, but that it can easily combine "when to make the change" and "whether it remains compatible afterward" into a single approval. The former is a coordination issue, while the latter must be supported jointly by the public entry point, contrasting inputs, and a replayed run.

The meeting did not rule out narrowing the use of the old entry point in the future. What was rejected was treating the window itself as compatibility evidence. For reviewed examples, the current entry point can continue to be retained; for unreviewed calls, this decision should not be used to accept their adjustment results by default.

## The Old Entry Point and Rollback

The old entry point is not a backup to be temporarily enabled only when a failure occurs. It is part of this choice: if any adjustment causes a discrepancy in the public text output of existing calls, first stop expanding the cutover scope and return to the old entry point to confirm whether the discrepancy disappears. Only if the discrepancy disappears under the old entry point may examination of the adjusted path continue; if the same phenomenon also occurs under the old entry point, it cannot be attributed directly to the window or entry-point change.

The rollback action remains limited: restore the old entry point to handle affected calls, retain the input and output that triggered the rollback, and restart the review from that input. This round did not establish a classification of all possible recovery scenarios or predefine handling for every query construct. The existing materials are sufficient only to specify a point at which checking can restart, not to create a runbook covering every exception.

This decision also sets no fixed deadline for how long the old entry point will be retained. The retention period should change in line with checks of public behavior for the specific scope of calls. Converting confirmation not yet obtained into a date would make the window appear more certain than the actual evidence warrants.

## Boundaries of the Coordination Record

The public interface owner maintains the entry-point assessments and rollback conditions. Coordination records should separate reviewed examples from scopes for which adjustments are only planned: the former may include run results, while the latter should record only the proposed window and inputs that still need checking. Mixing the two in the same cutover table would mislead readers into thinking that every planned item has already passed compatibility verification.

Cutover details that need to be handed over are kept in DOC-52. This page retains the options, the decisions made, and the rationales that were not accepted, rather than being rewritten as migration steps. If new call discrepancies are discovered during handoff, new review material should be created; it may change future window arrangements, but it cannot retroactively change the scope expressed by the approved examples.

Coordination records need to retain the actual impacts: which calls are still handled by the current entry point, which attempts remain at the preparation stage because replay results are missing, and whether any rollback has occurred. Actual impacts here refer only to changes in entry-point status and cutover status, without mixing speculation about internal causes into the record.

## Reservations

One reasonable objection remains: retaining both entry points over the long term will increase the maintenance burden and make the window seem to have no natural endpoint. This objection has been retained, not dismissed as an irrelevant concern. It is simply insufficient to overturn the current choice. The maintenance burden is a visible cost; expanding the scope without checking may change the boundaries of call behavior. A shared schedule alone cannot offset one against the other.

Another unresolved issue is how extensive the coverage of contrasting inputs should be. The existing review covers only two specific textual forms and has not produced a catalog of all query constructs. Any later expansion of the window should add inputs directly related to the proposed adjustment, rather than repeatedly collecting the same successful output.

This round's conclusion remains narrow: query-model continues as the public entry point; the window carries no independent compatibility approval; the old entry point is retained for rollback and comparison. New review results can support new arrangements, but before those arrangements are changed, the portion of public behavior they actually cover should first be documented.

server-runtime is one location checked in this round of review, used to verify the call relationships around the entry. It cannot confirm business-side behavior on behalf of the user, nor can it write recovery actions for the module.

The first batch should include only users that can roll back on their own. They must be able to explain three things: where the original call enters; what they first saw after switching to the candidate path; and how to return to the old entry if it fails. If the callers have not been fully inventoried, or the recovery action has not been clearly documented, the migration remains in progress.

Do not guess attributions for cross-layer issues here. During the handoff, include the call entry, the first visible result, and the next person taking over. versions.body:
# Public Entry Point Switch Handoff Process

The maintenance transition for the public entry point was once understood to mean getting the server-runtime side in order, then notifying consumers to change entry points. The approach retained after review is the opposite: first identify calls still using the old entry point, then have one consumer that can roll back independently try the switch. Checking the files is still useful, but it does not mark completion of the handoff.

This handoff tracks two relationships in parallel. The old entry point answers "where do existing calls still come in?" The candidate path answers "who is already willing and able to switch?" Both coexist for a period of time; identifying a consumer does not mean that consumer has migrated.

```text
Old entry point ──> Known consumers ──> server-runtime lookup
  │
  └── Keep the original call site

Candidate path ──> Consumers that can roll back independently ──> First observable result
                    │
                    └── Restore the old entry point on failure
```

Start by compiling the old-entry inventory. Each record covers just one specific consumer and includes at least the entry point name, where the call enters, and the first result that the module can currently confirm. That result is not a conclusion about the entire cross-layer call chain; it may simply be that calls still arrive, that the return shape changes, or that the original entry point is no longer traversed. These records let the next person taking over distinguish where a change occurred after entry point selection.

Do not make bulk moves based on directory or module names during the inventory. Even if two calls both go through server-runtime, they may be in different states: one may already have a clear rollback action, while the other has only had its old entry point confirmed. The former can enter a trial; the latter stays in the inventory. Combining them would mislead later maintainers into thinking the old path is no longer needed.

Keep the old entry point until each consumer's rollback point is documented. "Keep" is not a long-term compatibility commitment here; it means calls that have not entered a trial still have their original entry point available. If only a segment of adjacent calls has been confirmed from the runtime side, do not disable the old entry point on that basis; confirm the caller population and rollback actions separately.

## Initial Trial Runs

Start the candidate-path trials with consumers that can roll back independently. This means the module can restore its own entry point selection to the old path without waiting for changes in other modules. Before the trial, that consumer should have documented the original entry point, the first result seen after the switch, and the entry point selection to restore when rolling back.

The first batch is not intended to cover every module. Its only job is to run a real call through the candidate path with a rollback point in place. During the trial, change only this module's entry point selection. Do not also tidy up other modules' integration relationships, and do not declare the public entry point switch complete just because local behavior meets expectations. While the old entry point and candidate path coexist, the records should show which path each trial consumer has selected.

Some consumers can already provide a first observable result but have no way to roll back independently. Those records are still valuable, but those consumers do not move onto the candidate path. This shows that the call relationship has been identified, not that the risks of switching are under control. Conversely, even if the rollback actions are fully documented, do not expand the trial scope if actual use of the old entry point has not yet been fully verified.

## Writing the Handoff Record

Each module owner documents only the scope of behavior they can confirm. The record can be short, but each consumer record should keep these details together:

- Which entry point the call currently uses;
- The first result seen after the switch;
- Up to which layer this module can confirm behavior;
- Which old entry point to return to when rolling back;
- Who the next explicitly identified person to take over is when crossing this module's boundary.

Cross-layer issues must include the call entry point, the first observable result, and the next explicitly identified person to take over. Leaving only "there's a problem with runtime" is not enough to proceed, because the person taking over cannot see which call brought in the issue or tell whether the change following the trial has already occurred. Stop the record there; do not preemptively diagnose the cause for the next layer.

The handoff table can retain incomplete items. If a consumer's old entry point has been found but its rollback action has not yet been documented, marking it as not yet in a trial is more accurate than forcing it onto the candidate path. An in-migration status is not a failure; it means one of two pieces is still missing: the consumer's caller population or its rollback conditions.

## Restoring the Old Path

Document the rollback action before the trial. If the trial fails, carry it out using that consumer's own entry point selection. Rolling back does not mean deleting the trial record: keep both the first observable result and the original call site, since they show how far the candidate path actually got. After rolling back, the consumer returns to the old-entry inventory. If it enters another trial later, the investigation can resume from the earliest change observed on the previous attempt.

Other modules do not automatically roll back with it. If the observed behavior has already crossed this module's boundary, first fill in the local entry point and result, then hand it off to the next person identified in the record. The old path is only the rollback point confirmed by the consumer running this trial, not the default answer to every cross-layer issue.

DOC-53 contain local trace-back notes on finding the actual entry point starting from react-integration. Continue there if you need to trace further along that object; this document maintains the handoff relationships between the old-entry inventory, candidate-path trials, and rollback actions.

The migration remains in progress. Continue filling out the known-consumer inventory based on actual calls; the candidate path accepts only calls that can be rolled back independently.

## Follow just one call edge

After choosing a direct caller, review the segment connecting it to the public entry point, then use the original execution records to confirm that it actually participated in this integration. Do not reverse that order: first follow the entry point to the caller, then check whether the execution records can still connect that path to the team's public entry point maintenance. A similar name appearing in a single execution record is not enough to stand in for a call edge.

The first real consumer is the stopping point. At that point, the record should show actual use of public entry point maintenance, not just an import or placement in a neighboring directory. The old approach did not trace into the consumer or count files beyond the consumer as part of react-integration.

## Boundaries retained

If the caller is no longer directly connected to the public entry point, or the execution records don't match this chain, return to the public entry point and re-establish the path. Stop where an ownership question needs another maintainer's answer; don't use same-named files to fill in a conclusion.

The judgment at the time was that using `vite.config.ts` as the first landmark for tracing back was the simplest approach. That judgment is retained here to explain why the old entry point was traced this way; it did not become a fixed file convention for maintaining the team's public entry point.

# On-Call Procedure for Shared Maintenance Intake

When a report comes in from the field, capture the evidence first, then decide where to route it. The connection-transport version, unedited results, and original execution record should be kept in the same maintenance record. This is not about naming the problem up front; it lets the next person see which entry point the report first reached and what result appeared first.

Screenshots, secondhand accounts, and excerpts someone has already interpreted can go further down the record. They often show what the sender was looking at at the time, but must not replace the original record. If a report has been forwarded multiple times, don't combine different people's summaries into one conclusion. If the version, results, and call entry point come from different forwards, label them separately rather than treating them as a single occurrence.

## Pin down what's visible first

Start by finding the call entry point. This means the actual step that entered the maintenance scope, not a summary such as "there's a connection problem." Then record the first visible result: it may not be the final error, and it does not need to be interpreted as the root cause. The entry point and first result let the person taking over start in the same place, without having to reconstruct the sequence of events from a secondhand account.

If no version is specified, ask for it first. If the version in the message doesn't line up with the attached results, keep both and note that they cannot yet be matched. Even if all you have is a cropped screenshot, you can still log it, but that record only establishes that the result shown in the screenshot was seen; it cannot be used to assign a particular module owner. If the original execution record has not yet been obtained, explicitly mark it as missing. Don't fill in the intervening steps with the maintenance team's guesses.

Handle the two types of text that appear together in a message separately: results the caller actually received are field evidence; cross-layer relationships the maintenance team infers from those results are still guesses. The former can continue with the handoff package; the latter must not become confirmed boundaries just because they have been forwarded. That way, even if the assessment changes later, the initial observations remain available for review.

## The first routing decision

The on-call person is responsible for the first routing decision, not for completing attribution for cross-layer issues. The first routing decision means handing the evidence to the next stage once the entry point and results available so far are enough to identify who should review that stage. It does not declare other modules unrelated, or settle the scope of impact on behalf of the long-term owner.

If the results fall within a single module, and both the call entry point and the observed behavior line up with it, hand off to that module's owner. In the handoff, preserve the connection-transport version, raw results, call entry point, first visible result, and already confirmed behavioral boundaries in the order received. Leave unconfirmed boundaries explicitly unconfirmed; don't turn them into conclusions just to make the handoff look complete.

If the results involve multiple modules, the handoff package must also name a specific person to take over next. This is the person who will actually continue reviewing the next part of the evidence, not a generic team name. If that person cannot be found yet, leave the record at the team's shared intake. Add the entry point or identify the person taking over before forwarding further. For messages with no entry point, ask for the steps that led to the issue and the original execution record. If all you have is the final error, first go back to the first visible result before that error.

An owner's reply of "This isn't my module" does not mean the earlier evidence can be deleted. Keep the original handoff and append the reason for withdrawing it and the new handoff direction. If the original handoff was based only on a guess that later proved invalid, keep that guess in its original place as well, so later readers don't mistakenly think that routing decision never happened in the first place.

## When to stop

If continuing the investigation requires broader permissions, the on-call person must stop at the confirmed entry point, not bypass permissions to fill in the assessment. If validation requires changing public behavior, do not treat a change made for validation as a routine troubleshooting step either. Also stop if proceeding would mean deciding scope on behalf of the long-term owner, or if the sender asks for unconfirmed cross-layer relationships to be written directly as conclusions.

When stopping, leave at least three things in the record: the call entry point confirmed so far, the missing evidence, and who needs to take over next. There is no need to list every unknown here; just make clear which one is blocking the routing decision. Don't fill in missing versions, entry points, or behavioral boundaries with guesses just because the record needs to be handed off.

Rollback applies only to routing actions taken by the on-call person, not to the behavior observed in the field itself. Stop forwarding, retain the original record, and state which entry point you are rolling back to. When handing off again, reuse the originals and add only the new person taking over and the boundaries confirmed later. If public behavior or permissions still need to change, remain at the stopping point and wait for the long-term owner's decision.

## Review addendum

The review added an exception involving two easily conflated types of content: within the same message, the caller's results can go into the handoff first, but the maintenance team's guesses cannot be upgraded to confirmed facts along with them. Only after an owner explicitly confirms their own module's behavioral boundaries should that portion be moved into the confirmed information. The cross-layer portion remains for the next person to handle with the same original evidence.

If it later turns out that the first routing decision was wrong, correct the handoff direction, not the original results. The maintenance record only needs to retain the old direction, the reason for withdrawing it, and the new person taking over. That way, the on-call shift leaves behind field evidence that someone can continue working with, rather than a single account assembled after the fact.
